title: Bioinformatics with R
text:
Before we start
Welcome to the Bioinformatics and Data Analysis using R tutorial series. This course will guide you through analysing gene expression data from a real research study investigating Human African Trypanosomiasis (HAT).

What you’ll need

R and RStudio: Make sure you have the latest versions installed
Required packages: We’ll use DESeq2, ggplot2, pheatmap, and several Bioconductor packages
Data files: The CSV files containing count data and sample metadata
A text editor: For keeping notes as you progress through tutorials



How to use this book
Each chapter builds on the previous one, introducing new concepts gradually. Start with Chapter 1 (Introduction to Bioinformatics) and work through in order. Feel free to revisit earlier chapters if you need to refresh your memory on R basics.


About the HAT dataset
Throughout this course, we’ll analyse data from a comparative study of gene expression in: - Control samples: Healthy individuals (not infected) - SERO TL+ samples: People with serology-positive status (infected but asymptomatic) - HAT samples: Patients with symptomatic Human African Trypanosomiasis
Our focus will be on comparing HAT versus SERO TL+ samples to understand how gene expression changes with disease progression.


Getting help
If you get stuck: 1. Check the code carefully for typos 2. Make sure all required packages are installed 3. Review the relevant section in an earlier chapter 4. Try running the diagnostic commands we provide
Good luck, and enjoy your journey into bioinformatics!

1.2 R and RStudio are different
R is the programming language and software that runs your analysis. RStudio is an integrated development environment (IDE): a user-friendly application for writing R code, running it, viewing plots, managing files, and getting help.
You need to install both, but you will normally open RStudio. RStudio uses R in the background. Installing RStudio without installing R first will not give you a working R setup.

1.6 Understand the RStudio layout
RStudio is usually divided into four panes:

Source: write and save scripts and Quarto documents
Environment: inspect objects currently held in memory
Console: run commands and read output
Files, Plots, Packages, Help: browse files, view figures, manage packages, and read documentation

The Source pane may not appear until you open a script. That is normal. Open one with File > New File > R Script.
To run the current line or a selected block from a script:

1.7 Create a project for this course
For these tutorials, create an RStudio Project and choose a location on your device where you can easily find it again (e.g. Documents or Home). Using a project keeps all of your scripts, data files and output files together in one place. It also sets R to look for files within the project folder automatically (relative file paths), so you do not need to specify their full location on your computer. This makes your code easier to share and move between computers, and less likely to produce “file not found” errors.
 
When the project is open, its name appears near the top right of RStudio. Open the .Rproj file or select the project from RStudio’s recent-projects menu when you return to it. Open the project before opening a script so that relative file paths work as expected.

1.9 Setting up your project folder
Every analysis needs organised output folders to help with reproducibility and reporting. For these tutorials, we need to create some results folders in our main project folder called tables, figures and objects. You can do this in Windows Explorer or Mac Finder, or you can even use R:






TipRun this setup code



The following statements create the folders required later in the chapter Run them from your script, but you do not need to understand or memorise every argument yet.



dir.create("tables", showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create("objects", showWarnings = FALSE)

These statements check if the folders already exist (if they do, they won’t complain) and create them if they don’t. The showWarnings = FALSE prevents “folder already exists” messages from cluttering your console. You can run this code to create the output folders but you do not need to memorise or reproduce it independently.
Your project should now look something a bit like this:
HAT_analysis/
├── figures/
├── tables/
├── objects/
├── HAT_analysis.Rproj
├── human_annotations_from_orgHs.csv
├── m_sample_counts.csv
└── m_sample_info.csv







ImportantKeep data and code organised



For the HAT tutorials, keep the data files in the project folder used by the workbook. Do not rename the supplied files unless you also update the code. Avoid opening CSV files in Excel and saving them again: Excel can change identifiers, formatting, or missing values.

1.10 Set useful RStudio defaults
R objects exist only in the current session unless you save them explicitly. To make analyses easier to reproduce:

Open Tools > Global Options on Windows, or RStudio > Settings on macOS.
In the General settings, set Restore most recently opened project at startup according to your preference.
Set Save workspace to .RData on exit to Never.
Turn off Restore .RData into workspace at startup if it is available.

Save your scripts and exported results, not an automatically saved workspace. Starting with a clean session makes it easier to tell which objects your code actually creates.

1.11 Install an R package
R includes many basic functions, but specialist analyses use additional packages. Install a package once, from the Console:

install.packages("ggplot2")

Load it at the start of each new R session:

library(ggplot2)

Do not put install.packages() in an analysis script that you will run repeatedly. It is an installation step, not an analysis step.
The following code will install all the libraries we will need in these tutorials, you just need to run it once:

install.packages("ggplot2")
install.packages("ggrepel")

Many bioinformatics packages are distributed through Bioconductor. This is a specialist software repository for genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic and other biological data analysis tools. It provides a large collection of interoperable packages that are widely used in modern bioinformatics workflows.
To install Bioconductor packages, we first install the BiocManager package from CRAN. We can then use BiocManager::install() to install packages (e.g. DESeq2).

install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("DESeq2")

As with CRAN packages, installation only needs to be performed once. After installation, load the package at the start of each R session:  

library(DESeq2)

RStudio says that R cannot be found
Close and reopen RStudio. If the problem remains, check that base R was installed separately and that you downloaded the installer for your operating system.

2.3 Creating an analysis script
Before we begin importing data, create a new R Script and save it in your project folder with an understandable filename (e.g. HAT_analysis.R). You can do this by selecting: File → New File → R Script and then saving the file in your project folder.



Creating a new R script in RStudio


Why do this? Every statement that you run during an analysis should be recorded in a script. This is a key component of reproducible research. A good analysis should be understandable and repeatable by both you and other researchers. Although it is possible to work interactively by typing statements directly into the console, those statements are easily lost once RStudio is closed.
By saving your code in a script, you create a permanent record of:

How the data were imported
How the data were processed
Which statistical analyses were performed
How tables and figures were generated

Over the course of these tutorials, you will build up your script to create a complete record of your analysis workflow. Make sure you save your script often to avoid losing any work.

title: 2  Getting Started with the HAT dataset
text:
2.4 Importing and inspecting data files
The first step in any analysis is getting your data into R. We have two files:

Count data (m_sample_counts.csv): rows are genes labelled with stable Ensembl IDs, columns are samples and each cell is the number of sequencing reads or fragments assigned to that gene in that sample
Sample metadata (m_sample_info.csv): rows are samples, columns are variables (e.g. disease status, sex, age)







TipTry it yourself: Predict before you import



Open m_sample_counts.csv and m_sample_info.csv in a text editor before running any R code (you can also use Excel but do not overwrite the original .csv files).

Which column do you think will become the row names of each table once loaded into R?
Are the values in m_sample_counts.csv whole numbers or decimals? Why might that matter for later analysis?
How many metadata columns does m_sample_info.csv have, and which one records the treatment group?



Now, let’s load these files into RStudio. We could use the Import dataset menu item but as we want our workflow to be recorded and reproducible, it would be best to use the script window. Let’s import the sample metadata first (the patient information).

sample_info <- read.csv(
  "m_sample_info.csv",
  header = TRUE,
  row.names = 1
)

To actually run this code, place the cursor anywhere inside the complete statement and click Run, or select all lines of the statement and click Run. In RStudio, you can also use Ctrl + Enter. If the console displays + instead of >, R is usually waiting for the rest of an incomplete statement, often because a closing parenthesis or quotation mark is missing.






NoteMulti-line statements



This statement could also be written on a single line as sample_info <- read.csv("m_sample_info.csv",header = TRUE,row.names = 1) but R statements do not have to fit on a single line. If R reaches the end of a line while the parentheses ( is still open, it will continue until it reaches the matching closing parenthesis ). A useful style that helps with readability is to place the opening function call on the first line, indent each argument and place the closing parenthesis on its own line.


What just happened:

read.csv() reads a CSV file into an R data frame object
header = TRUE means the first row contains column names
row.names = 1 means the first column becomes the row names (gene IDs or sample IDs)







TipTry it yourself: Data import practice



How would you import the sample count data into a data frame called count_data? Try this without looking back first but if you get stuck, refer to the previous example or open the solution below.








TipSolution






count_data <- read.csv(
  "m_sample_counts.csv",
  header = TRUE,
  row.names = 1
)




Convert the count data to a matrix
We now need to perform one additional step because of how R represents tabular data and because several downstream tools expect a numeric matrix.
The read.csv() function imports the sample counts as a data frame, which is useful for storing tabular data because different columns can contain different types of information, like numbers, text or categories. You can think of it like an Excel worksheet. However, many downstream tools expect the data to be just one type (e.g. numbers) so they can make various assumptions to speed up analysis. R has a special type of object called a matrix to store these single-type data. To convert count_data into a matrix, use:

count_data <- as.matrix(count_data)

This statement replaces the data-frame version of count_data with a matrix version. In this case, that is intentional because the downstream analysis expects a numeric matrix.

text:
2.5 Check that the data were imported correctly
Before continuing, we should check that the two files were imported as expected and that they describe the same samples. Finding problems now prevents counts from being matched to the wrong sample information later.

2.5.1 Check the dimensions
The dim() function reports the number of rows and columns in an object.
# Dimensions are reported as: rows, columns
dim(count_data)
dim(sample_info)
In count_data, the rows represent genes and the columns represent samples. In sample_info, the rows represent samples and the columns describe those samples.






TipTry it yourself: Interpret the output




How many genes and samples are in count_data?
How many samples are in sample_info?
Does the number of columns in count_data match the number of rows in sample_info?









TipSolution






There are 65,217 genes across 21 samples.
There are 21 samples with 6 types of metadata.
There are 21 columns in count_data and 21 rows in sample_info.






2.5.2 Check the row and column names
R objects can have names attached to their rows and columns. We can retrieve these using rownames() and colnames().
# Display the first few gene identifiers
head(rownames(count_data))

# Display the sample identifiers
colnames(count_data)
rownames(sample_info)

# Display the metadata variable names
colnames(sample_info)


2.5.3 Check that the samples match
Samples are stored as columns in count_data and as rows in sample_info. We therefore need to check whether colnames(count_data) and rownames(sample_info) contain the same identifiers in the same order. We could check them manually but we can save time with the identical() function that checks whether two objects contain the same values in the same order.

# check whether row names and column names match in the two data objects
identical(
  colnames(count_data),
  rownames(sample_info)
)

[1] TRUE


A result of TRUE confirms that the sample identifiers match and are in the same order.






NoteComments



You may have noticed that some lines in the code begin with a hash symbol, #. These lines are called comments.
R ignores everything after # on that line. Comments are written for people reading the code and are not treated as instructions for R.
Comments can help us:

explain the purpose of a section of code
record why an analytic decision was made
make a script easier to navigate
help someone else understand and reuse our analysis
remind our future selves what the code was intended to do

A useful comment normally explains why a function is being run or what a group of statements is intended to achieve. It should not simply repeat something that is already obvious from the code.
For example, this comment is not especially helpful:
# Use dim on count_data
dim(count_data)
This version better explains the purpose of the statement at this point in the script:
# Confirm the number of imported genes (rows) and samples (columns) 
dim(count_data)
Comments should be useful but concise. Too many comments can make a script harder to read, particularly when every simple function has a comment that merely repeats the code.








TipTry it yourself: Commenting practice



Think of some comments to add to your previous import and as.matrix() lines that would be useful to explain what they are doing and why.

2.6 Indexing and subsetting
Modern biological datasets can contain thousands of variables (e.g. genes) and samples. We don’t always want to examine or analyse every value at the same time. Instead, we often need to select:

one particular gene
a group of genes
one or more samples
a metadata variable, such as status group
samples or genes that meet a particular condition

Selecting part of an R object is called subsetting and indexing tells R which rows, columns, or individual values we want to select. For a matrix or data frame, values are selected using square brackets:
object[rows, columns]
The comma separates the row selection from the column selection:

before the comma specifies the rows
after the comma specifies the columns
leaving one side empty means selecting all rows or all columns


2.6.1 Selecting data by position
We can select rows and columns according to their numerical positions.
This can be difficult to follow at first, so let’s practice using a small example matrix containing two genes and three samples. Imagine that this matrix is stored in an object called small_matrix. You do not need to enter or run these statements.
        sample_1 sample_2 sample_3
gene_A    5         0         8
gene_B    2         4         1

small_matrix[2, 3]

sample_1 sample_2 sample_3 
       5        0        8

     0      4 

small_matrix[2, 3]
[1] 1

       sample_2 sample_3
gene_A        0        8
gene_B        4        1



Let’s try it out on the main sample count set:

# Select the first gene across all samples
count_data[1, ]

  h1.1   h1.2   h1.3   h1.5   h2.2   h2.3   h2.4   h2.5   h2.6  shi.1  shi.2 
    11     10      5      8      2      4     15      7      6      6      1 
 slo.1  slo.5  slo.6  slo.7 ctrl.2 ctrl.3 ctrl.6 ctrl.7 ctrl.8 ctrl.9 
    11      0      3      7     16      3      5     14     12      7 

# Select the first gene of the third sample
count_data[1, 3]

[1] 5

# Select the first gene of the first three samples
count_data[1, 1:3]

h1.1 h1.2 h1.3 
  11   10    5 


In the first statement, 1 selects the first row and the blank space means all the columns are selected.
count_data[1, ]
In the second statement, 1 selects the first row and 3 selects the third column.
count_data[1, 3]
In the third statement, 1:3 creates the sequence 1, 2, 3. The statement therefore selects the first gene and the first three sample columns:
count_data[1, 1:3]
Selecting by position is useful when exploring a dataset. However, positions can change if rows or columns are added, removed or rearranged, so be careful.






ImportantDebugging an indexing error



Errors are a normal part of scripting. The following statement was intended to select the value in the first row and third column of count_data, but it contains an error.
Enter this statement temporarily, run it, and then correct it immediately. Do not leave the erroneous version in your completed script.
count_data[1 3]

Which part of the indexing structure is missing?
Correct the statement and run it again. Which part of the error message or indexing structure helped you identify the problem?
Check that the corrected statement returns one value.









TipTry it yourself: Solution





The comma separating the row selection from the column selection is missing. Without the comma, R cannot interpret 1 3 as a valid indexing expression and states there is an unexpected numeric constant. The corrected statement is:

count_data[1, 3]

[1] 5







2.6.2 Selecting data by name
We can also select rows and columns using their names. Again, we’ll practice using the small example matrix containing two genes and three samples. You do not need to enter or run these statements.
        sample_1 sample_2 sample_3
gene_A    5         0         8
gene_B    2         4         1






TipTry it yourself: Predict what will happen



For each expression, predict what will be displayed from the small matrix:
small_matrix["gene_B", ]
small_matrix[, "sample_3"]
small_matrix["gene_B", "sample_2"]








TipSolution





Compare the output with your prediction. If they differ, identify whether the problem involved the row position, column position, comma or use of a name.
small_matrix["gene_B", ]
       sample_1 sample_2 sample_3
gene_B        2        4        1

small_matrix[, "sample_3"]
[1] 8 1

We can use the table() function with indexing and subsetting to help understand the design of the experiment. For example, to see a summary of the status of different groups in our dataset:

ctrl  hat sero 
   6    9    6 


Our dataset has three groups: controls, SERO TL+ (asymptomatic carriers) and HAT (symptomatic carriers). We will retain all three groups in the dataset, although some later analyses will focus specifically on the HAT-versus-SERO TL+ comparison.






TipTry it yourself: More indexing practice

Why do you think it has this distribution in the study?








TipSolution

 m 
21 


For this initial analysis, we are only focusing on male samples. Possible reasons for analysing a single sex include sampling limitations or an attempt to reduce variation associated with sex. We will return to the complete dataset later to explore the effect of sex and consider how including it changes the analysis.

What could happen if sex affects gene expression but is ignored during the analysis?
Can results from the male-only analysis automatically be generalised to female participants?










TipPossible answers






If samples from different sexes were included but sex was ignored, differences associated with sex could be mistaken for differences associated with disease status. Sex could also increase variation within the study groups, making genuine differences between groups more difficult to detect.
The analysis can describe patterns in the male participants included in this study but it does not show that the same patterns occur in female participants. Female samples would need to be included before we could assess whether the findings are similar across sexes.

Age is a biological characteristic that could influence gene expression. It is therefore important to understand the ages represented in the study.

Does the study include a narrow or wide range of participant ages?
Why might age affect gene expression?
Why would it be useful for comparison groups to have similar age distributions?
If one group contained mainly younger participants and another mainly older participants, would it be easy to determine whether differences in gene expression were associated with age or group status?

youngest_age

oldest_age

title: 3  Sample-Level Summaries and Visualisation
text:
3.3 Sample quality metrics
Before differential-expression analysis, we will calculate the total number of counts in each sample. This provides an initial overview of sequencing depth and can identify samples with substantially more or fewer counts than the others. It does not determine whether a sample should be removed, but it can identify samples that merit further investigation.
Garbage In, Garbage Out

3.3.1 Creating a sample-summary table
We already have the information needed to create sample-level summaries, but it is spread across two objects:

count_data contains the gene counts for each sample
sample_info contains information describing each sample

We can use indexing and subsetting to combine selected information from these objects into a new data frame called sample_summary.
In this new table:

each row will represent one sample
each column will contain a different piece of information about that sample

Because the rows of sample_info are already in the same order as the columns of count_data, the first total count can be safely combined with the first metadata row, the second with the second, and so on. This is why it was important to check the order was identical.
Calculate the sample summaries
First, we will calculate the total number of counts in each sample.

3.3.1.1 Total counts
Because each column of count_data represents one sample, we can use the R function colSums() to calculate the total number of counts in each sample and store it as a vector (a vector is just a collection of values stored in a particular order):

total_counts <- colSums(count_data)
total_counts

    h1.1     h1.2     h1.3     h1.5     h2.2     h2.3     h2.4     h2.5 
33006582 26836411 25185951 25640193 33085881 24336818 27354946 25878192 
    h2.6    shi.1    shi.2    slo.1    slo.5    slo.6    slo.7   ctrl.2 
23931262 23679611 19319607 28703914 23477956 21106464 28895003 25778199 
  ctrl.3   ctrl.6   ctrl.7   ctrl.8   ctrl.9 
25244807 28741458 23853634 29319359 27009012 


In this analysis, we will use the total assigned count for each sample as its library size. Library size is important because samples with more counts generally provide more information about gene expression than samples with fewer counts. Large differences between samples may reflect differences in sequencing depth or sample quality, so library size is an important measure to examine before further analysis.
Create the new data frame
We can now use the data.frame() function to combine the sample information and calculated summaries:

sample_summary <- data.frame(
  sample_id = colnames(count_data),
  status = sample_info$status,
  total_counts = total_counts
)

The data.frame() function combines values of equal length to create a table. Each named argument creates one column:

sample_id contains the sample identifiers
status contains the experimental status
total_counts contains the library size

Because we previously confirmed that:
identical(
  rownames(sample_info),
  colnames(count_data)
)
returned TRUE, the status values are in the same order as the count summaries.
Inspect the summary table
Display the first few rows:

head(sample_summary)

     sample_id status total_counts
h1.1      h1.1    hat     33006582
h1.2      h1.2    hat     26836411
h1.3      h1.3    hat     25185951
h1.5      h1.5    hat     25640193
h2.2      h2.2    hat     33085881
h2.3      h2.3    hat     24336818


You should see one row per sample and three columns:

sample_id
status
total_counts







WarningCheck your work



The number of rows in sample_summary should equal the number of sample columns in count_data:

nrow(sample_summary) == ncol(count_data)

[1] TRUE


The result should be TRUE.


Save the summary table
The sample_summary object currently exists in the R Environment. We can also save it as a CSV file to the tables folder:

write.csv(
  x = sample_summary,
  file = "tables/sample_summary.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

title: 3  Sample-Level Summaries and Visualisation
text:
3.4 Visualising data quality
Visualisations can reveal differences between samples that are difficult to appreciate from tables of numbers. This can be an important quality assessment method to help spot issues before an analysis. We will be creating plots using the ggplot2 package (https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org) but first we have to load the package. To ensure this happens every time, we can add the library() call to the top of the script:

library(ggplot2)

ggplot2 uses a concept of layers that allows us to build up plots using a uniform language. We can start with the data and basic chart type, then add labels, colours and other visual improvements as we go on.
To begin with, let’s compare the total number of counts in each sample. This can provide an initial indication of sequencing depth and samples with substantially higher or lower total counts may need further investigation.

3.4.1 Creating a basic bar chart

library_size_plot <- ggplot(
  sample_summary,
  aes(x = sample_id, y = total_counts)
) +
  geom_col()

This code creates a plot and saves it as an R object called library_size_plot. Saving the plot as an object allows us to display it, modify it and save it as an image later. You can run the object name to display the plot:

library_size_plot








The plot has three main components:

ggplot(sample_summary, ...) specifies the data frame containing the data
aes(x = sample_id, y = total_counts) maps the sample identifiers and total counts to the plot axes
geom_col() draws one bar for each sample

The sample names are difficult to read along the horizontal axis, so we can add a coord_flip() layer to turn the plot sideways:

library_size_plot <- ggplot(
  sample_summary,
  aes(x = sample_id, y = total_counts)
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip()
  
library_size_plot














Note



When building up ggplot layers, the + must appear at the end of the preceding line so R knows the plot statement continues.


The existing plot is updated and the new version is saved back into library_size_plot. This changes how the values are displayed but does not change the data in sample_summary.
How would you interpret the plot? Compare your interpretation with a partner:

What are two possible reasons why a sample might have fewer total counts or a smaller library size?
Does a lower value necessarily mean that the sample is poor quality? What additional information would you want before excluding it?



3.4.2 Saving the bar chart
The plot currently exists as an object in the R Environment. To use the plot outside R, we can save it as an image using the ggsave() function. We need to specify the filename (including the figures output directory) and the plot we want to save:
ggsave(
  filename = "figures/total_counts_per_sample.png",
  plot = library_size_plot
)
Check that the image is in the right place in your project folder:
HAT_analysis/

└── figures/
      └── total_counts_per_sample.png

section: 3.5 How many genes have zero counts?
text:
3.5 How many genes have zero counts?
The library-size figure compares the total counts across samples. However, each total combines counts from thousands of genes. We will now look within a single sample to see what this summary hides.
A sample can have a large total count even if many of its genes have no recorded counts. We will therefore look within one sample and ask how many genes have a count of zero.
Remember that count_data contains genes in rows and samples in columns. First, we’ll use indexing and subsetting to select all the gene counts from sample “h1.1” and store them in a new vector called sample_h1_1_counts:

sample_h1_1_counts <- count_data[, "h1.1"]
head(sample_h1_1_counts)

ENSG00000000003 ENSG00000000005 ENSG00000000419 ENSG00000000457 ENSG00000000460 
             11               0             241             523              82 
ENSG00000000938 
          14035 


In count_data[, "h1.1"], the empty position before the comma selects all genes, while "h1.1" selects just that one sample.






TipTry it yourself: Make a prediction



Before continuing, discuss these questions with a partner.

Do you expect every gene to have at least one count?
Why might some genes have zero counts?
Does a count of zero necessarily mean that the gene is never expressed?
Would you expect every sample to have zero counts for exactly the same genes?









NotePossible answer






No. Many genes are expressed only in particular cells, life stages or biological conditions.
A gene may be inactive in the sampled material, expressed at a very low level, or affected by limitations in sampling, mapping or annotation.
No. A zero means that no counts were recorded for that gene in this sample. The gene may be expressed elsewhere or at a level too low to detect.
No. Biological differences and technical variation can produce different sets of zero-count genes among samples.





3.5.1 Identify zero-count genes
We can test every gene count in sample_h1_1_counts to determine whether its count is equal to zero using the equality operator (==). The comparison is performed separately for every gene. It produces TRUE when a gene has zero counts and FALSE when it has a non-zero count. These logical values are stored in a vector called is_zero_count.

is_zero_count <- sample_h1_1_counts == 0
head(is_zero_count)

ENSG00000000003 ENSG00000000005 ENSG00000000419 ENSG00000000457 ENSG00000000460 
          FALSE            TRUE           FALSE           FALSE           FALSE 
ENSG00000000938 
          FALSE 


We can count the TRUE values using sum() and store the value in number_zero_count_genes using:

number_zero_count_genes <- sum(is_zero_count)
number_zero_count_genes

[1] 35941


There are 65,217 genes in the dataset but we can make the code more reproducible by obtaining this value from count_data rather than hard-coding it. Because genes are stored in rows nrow(count_data) returns the total number of genes:

(number_zero_count_genes  / nrow(count_data)) * 100

[1] 55.10986








TipTry it yourself: Interpret the result




What percentage of genes have zero counts?
Is this higher or lower than you predicted?
What biological and technical explanations could account for these zeros?
Why should we avoid concluding that every zero-count gene is biologically inactive?









TipPossible answers






Approximately 55.1% of genes have zero counts in this sample:
Your answer will depend on your prediction. More than half of the genes have zero counts.
Biologically, some genes may be inactive in the sampled cells or condition. Technically, zero counts can also result from very low expression, limited sampling, unsuccessful mapping or incomplete annotation.
A zero means that no counts were recorded for that gene in this sample. It does not prove that the gene is never expressed. It may be expressed in another cell type or condition, or at a level too low to detect.




What does this summary hide?
The percentage tells us how many genes have zero counts, but it does not show how the remaining counts are distributed. It does not distinguish between non-zero counts such as:
1, 10, 100, 1,000 or 10,000
RNA-seq counts can span a very wide range, making their complete distribution difficult to display on an ordinary linear scale.
In the next chapter, we will learn how a mathematical transformation can make this distribution easier to visualise.

3.7 Optional extra activities
You have now completed the required activities for this chapter. The remaining activities are optional but valuable opportunities for further practice. You can attempt them now or return to them later.






TipOptional Activity 1: Find the samples with the largest and smallest library sizes



The library size of an RNA-seq sample is the total number of counts recorded for that sample. In our summary table, library size is stored in the total_counts column.
Samples with larger library sizes have more counts available for analysis. However, a larger library size does not necessarily mean that a sample is of higher quality. Library size is only one of several quality-control measurements.
Can you use subsetting to find the samples with the largest and smallest library sizes?
The R functions which.min() and which.max() may be useful but it is important to note that they return the position of the smallest or largest value, not the sample name. We will have to do some subsetting and indexing to find that out.








TipOne possible approach





One approach is to save the positions before using them to subset sample_summary:

index_min <- which.min(sample_summary$total_counts)
index_max <- which.max(sample_summary$total_counts)

sample_summary[index_min, c("sample_id", "total_counts")]

      sample_id total_counts
shi.2     shi.2     19319607

sample_summary[index_max, c("sample_id", "total_counts")]

     sample_id total_counts
h2.2      h2.2     33085881


Alternatively, you can perform each operation in one expression:

sample_summary[
  which.min(sample_summary$total_counts),
  c("sample_id", "total_counts")
]

      sample_id total_counts
shi.2     shi.2     19319607

sample_summary[
  which.max(sample_summary$total_counts),
  c("sample_id", "total_counts")
]

     sample_id total_counts
h2.2      h2.2     33085881











TipOptional Activity 2: Plot the number of detected genes



The plot generated previously in the tutorial shows the total number of counts for each sample. Another useful summary is the number of genes with at least one count in each sample. We can add this information to our sample_summary table as a detected_genes column using logical operators.
This can be a bit hard to follow so first we can use subsetting to examine a small part of the count matrix:

count_data[1:6, 1:4]

                 h1.1 h1.2  h1.3  h1.5
ENSG00000000003    11   10     5     8
ENSG00000000005     0    0     0     0
ENSG00000000419   241  107   271   236
ENSG00000000457   523  225   475   499
ENSG00000000460    82   52    70    95
ENSG00000000938 14035 8670 19712 16696


Now we can use the > operator to test whether each count is greater than zero:

count_data[1:6, 1:4] > 0

                 h1.1  h1.2  h1.3  h1.5
ENSG00000000003  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE
ENSG00000000005 FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE
ENSG00000000419  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE
ENSG00000000457  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE
ENSG00000000460  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE
ENSG00000000938  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE


R returns:

TRUE when a count is greater than zero
FALSE when a count is zero

When logical values like these are used in a numerical calculation, R treats TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0 so we can use colSums() to count the TRUE values in each sample column and store that as a vector:

detected_genes <- colSums(count_data > 0)
detected_genes

  h1.1   h1.2   h1.3   h1.5   h2.2   h2.3   h2.4   h2.5   h2.6  shi.1  shi.2 
 29276  27264  28994  29300  27650  28113  29202  29888  28854  25043  25853 
 slo.1  slo.5  slo.6  slo.7 ctrl.2 ctrl.3 ctrl.6 ctrl.7 ctrl.8 ctrl.9 
 28100  25602  27694  27943  30195  26031  28953  29127  29051  27271 


We can add this to sample_summary using:

sample_summary$detected_genes <- detected_genes
head(sample_summary)

     sample_id status total_counts detected_genes
h1.1      h1.1    hat     33006582          29276
h1.2      h1.2    hat     26836411          27264
h1.3      h1.3    hat     25185951          28994
h1.5      h1.5    hat     25640193          29300
h2.2      h2.2    hat     33085881          27650
h2.3      h2.3    hat     24336818          28113


A count greater than zero does not necessarily indicate strong or biologically meaningful expression. This is a simple sample-level summary.
Next, try to modify the ggplot code from the tutorial to:

create a new plot called detected_genes_plot
display detected_genes on the y-axis
show the completed plot
save the plot as figures/detected_genes_per_sample.png

After creating the plot, consider the following questions:

What does each bar represent?
Why might one sample have fewer detected genes than the others?
Would this measurement alone be enough to justify removing a sample from the analysis?









TipOne possible approach






detected_genes_plot <- ggplot(
  sample_summary,
  aes(x = sample_id, y = detected_genes)
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip()

detected_genes_plot









ggsave(
  filename = "figures/detected_genes_per_sample.png",
  plot = detected_genes_plot
)

Saving 7 x 5 in image


Each bar represents the number of genes with a non-zero count in one sample.
A sample might have fewer detected genes because of lower sequencing depth, reduced library complexity, poorer RNA quality, or a genuine biological difference.
This measurement alone is not sufficient to justify removing a sample. It should be considered alongside other quality-control measurements and the experimental metadata.

title: 4  Transforming and Reshaping Data

4.1 What you’ll learn
In Chapter 3, we calculated the total number of counts in each sample and created a bar chart comparing library sizes. This provided an initial overview of sequencing depth but reduced each sample to a single summary value.
In this chapter, you will examine how counts are distributed across the genes in each sample. You will transform a copy of the count matrix to make its wide range of values easier to visualise, reshape the transformed data into a format suitable for ggplot2, and create a boxplot comparing count distributions across samples.
You will then consider the boxplot alongside the library-size plot from Chapter 3. Using more than one summary provides stronger evidence when identifying samples that may require further investigation.

4.2 Continuing the analysis from Chapter 3
Open the same RStudio Project and the HAT_analysis.R script used in Chapter 3. Add the new code from this chapter below your existing code so that the script remains a reproducible record of the analysis.
If you have restarted R, rerun your script from the beginning. This should ensure count_data and sample_info are loaded and the right type of object, and that sample_summary exists with the correct columns.






TipRecap: Essential setup code





The following code recreates the objects needed in this chapter. You should already have most of it in your script from Chapters 2 and 3.

# Import sample information
sample_info <- read.csv(
  "m_sample_info.csv",
  header = TRUE,
  row.names = 1
)

# Import counts and convert them to a numeric matrix
count_data <- read.csv(
  "m_sample_counts.csv",
  header = TRUE,
  row.names = 1
)

count_data <- as.matrix(count_data)

# Create the sample summary table
total_counts <- colSums(count_data)
sample_summary <- data.frame(
  sample_id = colnames(count_data),
  status = sample_info$status,
  total_counts = total_counts
)

text:
4.3 Additional sample-quality control
In Chapter 3, we calculated total_counts as a sample-level summary and plotted it for each sample (you may also have prepared a detected_genes summary plot for each sample if you completed the Optional Activity).






NoteRecap: Total counts per sample plot




library(ggplot2)
read_plot <- ggplot(
  sample_summary,
  aes(x = sample_id, y = total_counts)
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip()
  
read_plot










The total-count plot is a useful quality-control summary, but it reduces a complete sample to a single number. If you completed the optional detected-gene activity, that plot also reduces each sample to one value.
These summaries make samples easy to compare, but they do not show how counts are distributed among the genes. For example, two samples could have the same total number of counts and a similar number of detected genes (genes with at least one observed count), but one sample might contain relatively even expression across many genes while the other is dominated by a smaller number of highly expressed genes. This is important because a sample dominated by a small number of highly expressed genes may reflect a technical problem or an important biological feature of the sample, and may affect the comparisons we make later. Plotting the distribution of counts gives us another way to identify samples that may need closer investigation before we begin the differential expression analysis. Remember:
Garbage In, Garbage Out.






TipTry it yourself: Interpret the raw gene-count distribution plot



In the image below, we have plotted the distribution of gene counts using the raw count data.

What makes this graph difficult to interpret?
Where do most of the observed counts appear on the scale?




raw_count_distributions.png










TipSolution





A small number of genes have much larger counts than most others. These are often genes that produce abundant RNA molecules, such as genes involved in protein synthesis, core cellular processes or specialised functions of the sampled tissue. In blood-derived samples, for example, haemoglobin transcripts can account for a substantial proportion of the observed counts unless reduced during library preparation using a depletion method. High counts do not automatically indicate a problem but these large values determine the scale of the count axis and make differences among most gene counts difficult to see. Conversely, zeroes may just mean that no fragments were assigned to that gene in that sample. It does not necessarily mean the gene is biologically absent or never expressed.

title: 4  Transforming and Reshaping Data
text:
4.4 Transforming the counts for visualisation
Biological data often contain values that span a very wide range. This is sometimes described as having a large dynamic range. In RNA-seq data, many genes may have zero or relatively few counts, while a smaller number of highly expressed genes may have thousands or even millions of counts. This pattern is common in bioinformatics because biological molecules are not usually present at similar abundances. Some transcripts are required in very large quantities, while others are produced only in particular cell types, under particular conditions or at much lower levels.
We can address this by transforming the values before plotting them. A transformation applies the same mathematical function to every value, producing a new representation of the data. It does not remove the largest values, but changes the spacing between values so that a wide range can be displayed more clearly.
A common transformation in bioinformatics is the base-2 logarithm that can be applied to a numerical object using the log2() R function. On a log2 scale, each increase of one unit represents a doubling. The figure below is a comparison of the linear and log2 scales. On the linear scale, small values are compressed near zero because the axis must accommodate values as large as 1,000. On the log2 scale, each equal interval represents a doubling, allowing both small and large values to be distinguished.



Comparison of values displayed on linear and log2 scales.








TipTry it yourself: Compare the linear and log2 scale




Why are values from 1 to 64 difficult to distinguish when the linear axis must also display much larger counts?
Does the log2 transformation change the order of the values, or only the spacing between them?









TipSolution






Values from 1 to 64 occupy only a small part of the linear axis because the plot must also accommodate much larger counts. As a result, these smaller values are compressed close together and are difficult to distinguish.
The transformation preserves the order of positive values but does not preserve their original distances. It compresses larger values more strongly than smaller values.




We can apply a log2 transformation to all the values in the count_data matrix into a new matrix called log_count_data using the statement:

log_count_data <- log2(count_data + 1)

Because we assign the transformed values to a new matrix, the original count_data matrix remains unchanged.






NoteWhy do we add 1?



Before applying the log2 transformation, we add a small value of 1 to every count. This is sometimes called adding a pseudocount. In R, log2(0) returns -Inf, representing negative infinity. These non-finite values would make this visualisation difficult to interpret. After adding one, a raw count of zero becomes log2(0 + 1), which is zero. This keeps zero counts at zero in the transformed copy and prevents -Inf values from being produced.
Remember, in Chapter 3 we found that approximately 55.1% of genes had zero counts in the first sample. We therefore cannot apply log2() directly without producing many -Inf values.








TipTry it yourself: Check that the matrix structure was preserved



The transformation should only change the count values but preserve the organisation of the matrix. The transformed matrix should therefore contain the same number of genes and samples, with the samples in the same order.
Run the following checks:

# Check that the matrices have the same dimensions
identical(
  dim(log_count_data),
  dim(count_data)
)

[1] TRUE

# Check that the sample identifiers remain in the same order
identical(
  colnames(log_count_data),
  colnames(count_data)
)

[1] TRUE


Both statements should return TRUE.
This confirms that log_count_data has the same dimensions and sample order as count_data. The values have changed, but their positions in the matrix have not.








WarningTransformed values are for visualisation only



The log2-transformed values are used only to make this exploratory plot easier to read. We will not use these values for filtering, modelling or differential expression testing.
Those later steps will use the original integer counts stored in count_data.


We have changed the values but not their positions. Next, we will change their positions but not their values by reshaping the data.

title: 4  Transforming and Reshaping Data
text:
4.5 Data formats and reshaping
The transformed counts are currently stored in a matrix because this is a convenient format for RNA-seq data. Each row represents a gene, each column represents a sample and each cell contains the transformed count for one gene in one sample. This arrangement is called wide format because the measurements from different samples are spread across separate columns:
Wide format is useful for storing the count data, but it is less convenient for creating this boxplot. To draw the plot, ggplot2 needs to know two things for every count:

the value of the count
the sample to which the count belongs

We will therefore need to reshape a copy of the data so that all the transformed counts are collected in one column and the corresponding sample names are recorded in another. This arrangement is called long format because the measurements from the different samples are collected into a single column:

Reshaping changes how the data are arranged but it does not recalculate or transform the count values. Reshaping is a common operation in bioinformatics because the same data may need to be organised differently for storage, visualisation and analysis.






TipTry it yourself: Predict the new shape



This can be difficult to follow at first, so let’s practice using the small example count matrix we used in Chapter 2:
         sample_1  sample_2  sample_3
gene_A          5         0         8
gene_B          2         4         1
The matrix is in wide format. Each gene is stored in a row and each sample has its own column.
Imagine that we convert this matrix to a data frame and then use stack() to reshape it into long format.
Before looking at the solution, answer the following questions:

How many count values are present in the wide data?
How many rows will the long data contain?
Which count values will appear in the first column?
Which sample ID should be associated with each count?

Remember that stack() works through the first sample column, followed by the second sample column and then the third.








TipSolution






The wide data contain six count values:

2 genes × 3 samples = 6 count values

After reshaping, the long data will contain six rows. Each row contains one count value and the sample from which it came.
stack() works down each sample column in turn. The values will therefore appear in this order 5, 2, 0, 4, 8, 1.
The counts and sample IDs will be arranged as follows:

count  sample_id
5           sample_1
2           sample_1
0           sample_2
4           sample_2
8           sample_3
1           sample_3



Reshaping the log2 matrix
The log2-transformed counts are currently stored as a matrix. Before using stack(), we have to convert the matrix to a data frame because the stack() function expects its input to be organised as a data frame:






TipTry it yourself: Convert the matrix into a data frame



In Chapter 2, we used the as.matrix() function to convert a data frame into a matrix:
count_data <- as.matrix(count_data)
We now want to convert a matrix in the opposite direction. The function for this is as.data.frame().
Use as.data.frame() to complete the statement below:
log_count_data_frame <- __________________________
Remember, the object we want to convert is called log_count_data. We don’t want to overwrite it so we will assign it to a new object called log_count_data_frame.








TipSolution






log_count_data_frame <- as.data.frame(log_count_data)




We now use the stack() function in R to reshape the wide format data frame into long format:

count_plot_data <- stack(log_count_data_frame)
head(count_plot_data)

     values  ind
1  3.584963 h1.1
2  0.000000 h1.1
3  7.918863 h1.1
4  9.033423 h1.1
5  6.375039 h1.1
6 13.776844 h1.1


By default, stack() names the columns values and ind, which isn’t very useful. We can replace those names with clearer ones using the colnames() function we have previously used:

colnames(count_plot_data) <- c(
  "log2_count",
  "sample_id"
)

head(count_plot_data)

  log2_count sample_id
1   3.584963      h1.1
2   0.000000      h1.1
3   7.918863      h1.1
4   9.033423      h1.1
5   6.375039      h1.1
6  13.776844      h1.1








Warning



The original count matrix contains one value for every gene–sample combination. Reshaping places each of these values in a separate row, so count_plot_data will contain more than one million rows.
This is expected. Use functions such as head(), dim() and nrow() to inspect the object rather than attempting to print the complete data frame.
The reshaped data retain every transformed count and its associated sample identifier. They do not retain the gene identifiers because these are not required for this sample-level boxplot. The original gene identifiers remain available in log_count_data and count_data.








NoteWhat does c() mean?



The c() function combines values into a vector. A vector is an ordered collection of values with the same basic type (like a list of numbers or a list of words). It is similar to one column in a spreadsheet.
Here, c() creates a character vector containing the two actual column names:
c("log2_count", "sample_id")
The complete statement assigns those names, in order, to the two columns of count_plot_data.








TipTry it yourself: Was every transformed count retained?



The number of rows in the long data should equal:
number of genes × number of samples
Run the following statements:

nrow(count_plot_data)

[1] 1369557

nrow(count_data) * ncol(count_data)

[1] 1369557



Do the two results match?
What does this confirm, and what does it not confirm?









TipSolution





The two values should match because every entry in the original matrix produces one row in the long data.
This confirms that the long data contain the expected number of transformed values. It does not prove that the values are unchanged or correctly associated with their sample identifiers.

text:
4.6 Create the gene-count distribution boxplot
We have now prepared the data in the structure needed for the plot. Each row of count_plot_data contains:

one transformed gene-count value in log2_count
the sample associated with that value in sample_id

This means that ggplot2 can group together all the transformed counts belonging to the same sample. It will use those values to create one boxplot for each sample.
Each boxplot summarises the distribution of transformed counts across all genes in that sample. It shows the typical values and their spread, allowing us to compare the overall count distributions between samples. The points beyond the whiskers represent individual gene counts, not outlier samples. They are not automatically measurement errors.
In Chapter 3, you built a plot using this general structure:
a_plot <- ggplot(
  data = a_data_frame,
  mapping = aes(
    x = an_x_variable,
    y = a_y_variable
  )
) +
  a_geom()
We will reuse that structure with the new long-format data but this time, instead of using geom_col() to create a bar chart, we will use geom_boxplot().






TipTry it yourself: Create a boxplot



Complete the code by replacing the blanks with the names below. Try this without looking back first. If you get stuck, open the solution.

count_plot_data
sample_id
log2_count

count_distribution_plot <- ggplot(
  ___________________,
  aes(x = __________, y = __________)
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip()

count_distribution_plot








TipSolution






count_distribution_plot <- ggplot(
  count_plot_data,
  aes(x = sample_id, y = log2_count)
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip()

count_distribution_plot











Compare your transformed boxplot with the raw-count distribution plot shown earlier. Because many genes have zero counts, the median and lower quartile of some samples may be zero. This is a feature of the data rather than a plotting error.

In which plot is it easier to see the boxes and compare the distributions between samples?
Why are most values compressed close to zero in the raw-count plot?
What has the log2 transformation changed about the appearance of the data?
Has the log2 transformation changed which values are relatively low or high?

The log2 transformation makes the distributions easier to visualise but samples are not expected to have identical distributions because genuine biological differences can alter gene expression. This plot can be used to identify broad or unexpected differences that should be investigated alongside other QC evidence.
The plot currently only exists as an object in the R Environment. To use the plot outside R, we can save it as an image using the ggsave() function. Try to recall the code from Chapter 3 to save the count_distribution_plot as count_distributions_per_sample.png into the figures/ output directory.






TipSolution






ggsave(
  filename = "figures/count_distributions_per_sample.png",
  plot = count_distribution_plot
)

Saving 7 x 5 in image

4.7 Combine the quality-control evidence
Let’s bring everything together and compare the count-distribution plot with the sample_summary table and the library-size plot from Chapter 3.

Are the count distributions broadly similar across the samples?
Do the samples with higher total counts also have noticeably different count distributions?
Does any sample appear consistently different across total counts and count distribution (or detected genes if you did the Optional Activity)?
Based on the evidence available, is there a clear reason to exclude any sample before continuing?
Why is it useful to examine several quality-control summaries rather than relying on only one?







TipBiological interpretation



Differences in these plots can reflect sequencing depth and composition as well as technical or biological differences. At this stage, treat them as descriptive prompts for further investigation, not as formal criteria for removing samples. Write a short conclusion explaining how you interpret them using the following structure (you could add it as a comment in your script to remind yourself):
# Overall, the samples show ______. Although there is some variation in ______, no sample appears ______ across all the quality-control summaries. We will therefore ______.








ImportantQC does not need to identify a failed sample



A quality-control assessment does not need to identify a failed sample. Finding no clear evidence of a problematic sample is also a useful result.

text:
4.8 Summary
In this chapter, you examined how gene counts are distributed within each sample. Raw RNA-seq counts span a wide range, which can make their distributions difficult to compare on a linear scale. You therefore created a log2-transformed copy of the count matrix for visualisation while preserving the original integer counts for later differential-expression analysis.
You then reshaped the transformed data from wide format, where each sample occupied a separate column, into long format, where each row contained one transformed count and its associated sample identifier. This allowed you to use ggplot2 to create a boxplot comparing count distributions across samples.

Transformation values change, structure remains
Reshaping structure changes, values remain

In this chapter, you:

created a log2-transformed copy of the count matrix using log2(count_data + 1)
explained why a pseudocount is added before transforming zero counts
confirmed that transformation preserved the dimensions of the count matrix
distinguished between wide-format and long-format data
converted the transformed matrix into a data frame
reshaped the transformed data using stack()
checked that the reshaped data contained the expected number of values
created a boxplot comparing count distributions across samples
combined evidence from the library-size and count-distribution plots
interpreted unusual patterns cautiously rather than automatically excluding samples

No single quality-control summary is sufficient to determine whether a sample should be removed. Differences between samples could reflect sequencing depth, sample composition, technical variation or genuine biology. Samples with unusual patterns should therefore be investigated using multiple sources of evidence.
The quality-control summaries provide no clear reason to exclude any samples at this stage. In the next Chapter 5, we will return to the original integer counts and use the sample groups in sample_info to test for differences in gene expression.

4.9 Optional extra activities
You have now completed the required activities for this chapter. The remaining activities are optional but valuable opportunities for further practice. You can attempt them now or return to them later.






TipOptional Activity 1: Compare different transformations



In this tutorial, we used log2 transformation to make a large range of RNA-seq counts easier to visualise. But there are also other ways to transform data that adjust the scale and represent the data differently.
Create two additional transformed versions of count_data:
log10_count_data <- log10(count_data + 1)

square_root_count_data <- sqrt(count_data)
Choose one or both of these transformed matrices and adapt the reshaping code from earlier to create a boxplot.
Compare the new plot with the log2 transformation plot.

How do the numerical axis values differ between the log2 and log10 plots?
Do log2 and log10 change the ordering or relative pattern of the counts?
How does the square-root plot differ visually from the logarithmic plots?
Why must the axis label state which transformation was applied?









TipOne possible approach





Log10-transformed counts:

log10_count_data <- log10(count_data + 1)

log10_count_data_frame <- as.data.frame(
  log10_count_data
)

log10_count_plot_data <- stack(
  log10_count_data_frame
)

colnames(log10_count_plot_data) <- c(
  "log10_count",
  "sample_id"
)

log10_count_distribution_plot <- ggplot(
  log10_count_plot_data,
  aes(
    x = sample_id,
    y = log10_count
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of gene counts in each sample",
    x = "Sample",
    y = "log10(count + 1)"
  )

log10_count_distribution_plot









Log2 and log10 produce different numerical scales because they use different bases. One is a constant rescaling of the other, so they preserve the same ordering and relative pattern among counts. The square-root transformation compresses the upper range less strongly than a logarithmic transformation.
The numerical values and axis units differ because the logarithms use different bases. The axis label must therefore state which transformation was used.
A square-root transformation also compresses the range of the counts but less strongly than either logarithmic transformation. It produces a plot that lies between the raw-count and log-transformed plots, making the smaller values easier to distinguish but the largest counts can still have a strong effect on the scale.
Because the numerical values and axis units differ between transformations, the axis label must always clearly state which transformation was used.

Square root-transformed counts:

square_root_count_data <- sqrt(count_data)

square_root_count_data_frame <- as.data.frame(
  square_root_count_data
)

square_root_count_plot_data <- stack(
  square_root_count_data_frame
)

colnames(square_root_count_plot_data) <- c(
  "sqrt_count",
  "sample_id"
)

square_root_count_plot <- ggplot(
  square_root_count_plot_data,
  aes(
    x = sample_id,
    y = sqrt_count
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of gene counts in each sample",
    x = "Sample",
    y = "sqrt(count)"
  )

square_root_count_plot

title: 5  Preparing Data for Differential-Expression Analysis
text:
5.1 What you’ll learn
In Chapter 4, you examined the distribution of gene counts within each sample. You created a log2(count + 1) transformed copy of the count matrix, reshaped it for plotting and compared the samples using boxplots. By combining this plot with the quality-control summaries from Chapter 3, you found no clear reason to exclude any samples at this stage.
In this session, we’ll ask whether gene expression differs between patients with symptomatic HAT and people classified as SERO TL+ (sometimes described as having latent infections). Remember, both groups are infected with trypanosome parasites but SERO TL+ individuals do not show an overt phenotype.
We will prepare the counts and sample information for DESeq2, construct and inspect a DESeqDataSet and filter out low-count genes. The next chapter will fit the model and extract the differential-expression contrast.
Before writing any code, it’s important to consider the biology. Discuss the following questions with a partner before revealing the solution:
crumbs: 5  Preparing Data for Differential-Expression Analysis

title: 5  Preparing Data for Differential-Expression Analysis
text:
What is the response being measured?
What is the explanatory variable?
What are the biological replicates?
What comparison will HAT versus SERO TL+ make?
What could this observational comparison show and what can it not establish?







TipSolution






The response is the number of RNA-seq counts assigned to each gene in each sample. These gene counts provide a measure of gene expression.
The explanatory variable is status, which places each biological sample into a group (hat, sero or ctrl).
The biological replicates are the independently collected samples from different people within each group. Genes and sequencing reads are measurements taken from these samples, not additional biological replicates.
It will compare gene expression in samples from the HAT group with gene expression in samples from the SERO TL+ group. For this comparison, a positive log2 fold change indicates higher estimated expression in HAT, while a negative log2 fold change indicates higher estimated expression in SERO.
The analysis can identify genes whose expression is associated with HAT or SERO status in these samples. It cannot establish that status directly caused the differences in gene expression. Other biological or technical differences between the groups could also contribute to the observed pattern.










NoteLearning outcomes



By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

verify that a count matrix and sample metadata are aligned
represent an experimental group as a factor and inspect its levels
explain the roles of countData, colData and design
construct and inspect a DESeqDataSet
filter genes using a logical condition and verify the result
save the filtered DESeqDataSet so it can be reloaded in the next chapter

5.2 Load the input data
Load the count matrix and sample information at the start of the session so the workflow can be run after restarting R.

count_data <- as.matrix(read.csv(
  "m_sample_counts.csv", header = TRUE, row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE
))

  "m_sample_info.csv", header = TRUE, row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE
)

For this session we will be using the DESeq2 R package so we need to load it using the library() function. You can add this to the top of your script with the other package imports, or place it before the next code block.

library(DESeq2)

section: 5.3 Representing the biological groups as a factor
text:
5.3 Representing the biological groups as a factor
In the HAT dataset, the status column contains the category labels ctrl, sero and hat. R can store these labels as ordinary text, but the statistical model needs to recognise that they represent distinct biological groups. We therefore have to convert status into a factor.
A factor is how R stores a variable made up of a fixed set of categories, such as biological groups. Unlike ordinary text, a factor tells R which categories exist so they can be used correctly in summaries, plots and statistical models.

sample_info$status <- factor(
  sample_info$status
)

levels(
  sample_info$status
)

[1] "ctrl" "hat"  "sero"








NoteFactor level order



The order of factor levels can affect how model coefficients are labelled. In this chapter, the direction of the biological comparison will be specified explicitly using a contrast, so we do not need to change the reference level to get the comparison we want.
crumbs: 5  Preparing Data for Differential-Expression Analysis

title: 5  Preparing Data for Differential-Expression Analysis
text:
5.4 Checking biological replication
Before constructing the model, we should understand how many biological samples are available for each status. The number of samples matters because DESeq2 uses the differences among samples within the same group to estimate biological variability.
Here, each column in the count matrix represents one biological sample. The genes and sequencing reads are measurements taken from those samples. They are not additional biological replicates.
As in Chapter 2, we can use the table() function to summarise the status column in sample_info to show the number of samples in each group.
table(sample_info$status)






TipTry it yourself: Interpret group replication




How many biological samples are in each group?
Are the groups balanced?
What is the replicate in this experiment: each gene, each read, or each person/sample?
Why do 30,000 genes not compensate for having relatively few samples?
Which group has the least information for estimating within-group variability?









TipSolution






There are 6 CTRL samples, 9 HAT samples and 6 SERO TL+ samples.
The groups are not completely balanced, because they do not all contain the same number of samples. HAT has three more samples than either CTRL or SERO TL+. This difference does not prevent DESeq2 from performing the analysis.
The biological replicates are the independently collected people or samples within each group. Each column of the count matrix represents one biological replicate. Genes and sequencing reads are measurements taken from those samples, not additional biological replicates.
The approximately 30,000 genes are measured repeatedly in the same set of biological samples. They provide information about many different genes, but they do not provide 30,000 independent observations of the difference between HAT and SERO TL+. Additional biological samples would provide more information about how much expression varies among people within each group.
CTRL and SERO TL+ have the fewest biological samples, with six each. For our planned HAT-versus-SERO TL+ comparison, SERO TL+ therefore provides less information about within-group variability than HAT. This may make estimates involving SERO TL+ less precise than they would be if more SERO TL+ samples were available.

title: 5  Preparing Data for Differential-Expression Analysis
text:
5.5 Constructing the DESeqDataSet
DESeq2 stores the information needed for differential expression analysis in an object called a DESeqDataSet. Keeping the information together helps ensure that the counts for each sample remain connected to the correct sample information and experimental design.
A DESeqDataSet contains three connected components:

countData the RNA-seq counts as a matrix (genes in rows and samples in columns)
colData information describing the samples (samples in rows and variables in columns)
design = the sample variable or variables included in the model

The design formula tells DESeq2 which sample variable should be included when explaining systematic differences in the counts.
For this analysis, the design formula is:
~ status
The tilde (~) introduces a model formula. Here, ~ status tells DESeq2 that the model should include differences associated with the levels of status.
This design includes all three status groups. It does not yet specify which two groups we want to compare. We will request the HAT-versus-SERO TL+ comparison later using results().

5.5.1 Complete the function call
We can construct the DESeqDataSet object we need using the DESeqDataSetFromMatrix() helper function from DESeq2.






TipTry it yourself: Complete the code



How would you use each of the following options once to fill in the blanks and complete the statement to build a DESeqDataSet with our HAT dataset:
count_data    sample_info    status
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
  countData = __________,
  colData = __________,
  design = ~ __________
)
Think about the type of information expected by each argument:

Which object contains the RNA-seq counts?
Which object describes the biological samples?
Which variable identifies the biological groups?









TipSolution






dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
  countData = count_data,
  colData = sample_info,
  design = ~ status
)


countData = count_data supplies the matrix of gene counts.
colData = sample_info supplies the information describing each sample.
design = ~ status tells DESeq2 to include the biological status groups in the model.










WarningMake sure to use the original counts



DESeq2 uses the original integer counts. The log2(count + 1) values created in Chapter 4 were used only for visualisation and must not be supplied to the model.
Make sure you are using countData = count_data and not the transformed log_count_data.


Creating a dds object organises the counts, sample information and design into one object to make sure it is in a format ready for DESeq2 to use. It has not yet fitted a statistical model or changed the original count values.

5.6 Check the information stored in dds
After constructing the dds object, we should check that it contains the correct counts, sample information and design.
DESeq2 provides accessor functions for retrieving these components:

counts() retrieves the count matrix
colData() retrieves the sample information
design() retrieves the design formula

We can use these functions to perform three brief checks before continuing.
Check the count matrix
The complete count matrix is large, so we will inspect only the first five genes and first four samples using the subsetting skills from Chapter 2:

counts(dds)[1:5, 1:4]

                h1.1 h1.2 h1.3 h1.5
ENSG00000000003   11   10    5    8
ENSG00000000005    0    0    0    0
ENSG00000000419  241  107  271  236
ENSG00000000457  523  225  475  499
ENSG00000000460   82   52   70   95

  counts(dds)[1:5, 1:4],
  count_data[1:5, 1:4]

[1] TRUE





Check the sample information
The colData() function retrieves the sample information stored in dds. DESeq2 stores this information in a specialised table that we can convert to a familiar data frame:

dds_sample_info <- as.data.frame(colData(dds))

head(dds_sample_info)

     status detailed_status sex age
h1.1    hat          hat_p1   m  34
h1.2    hat          hat_p1   m  30
h1.3    hat          hat_p1   m  20
h1.5    hat          hat_p1   m  18

Compare dds_sample_info with the original sample_info object.

Do the sample names appear in the same order?
Does each sample have the same status in both objects?
Why would a difference in sample order be a serious problem?









TipSolution






We can compare the row names of the two objects directly:


identical(
  rownames(dds_sample_info),
  rownames(sample_info)
)

[1] TRUE


This should return TRUE, confirming that the sample names appear in the same order.

We can compare the status values directly:


identical(
  as.character(dds_sample_info$status),
  as.character(sample_info$status)
)

[1] TRUE


This should return TRUE, confirming that each sample has the same status in both objects.

The columns of the count matrix and the rows of the sample information must describe the same samples in the same order. If their order differed, a sample’s counts could be associated with information from the wrong person. DESeq2 could then compare incorrectly labelled biological groups.




Check the model design
Finally, use design() to retrieve the model formula stored in dds:

design(dds)

~status


This confirms that status is the sample variable included in the model. It does not yet specify the HAT-versus-SERO TL+ comparison. We will define that comparison when we retrieve the model results.

text:
5.7 Apply a simple low-count filter
Before fitting the model, we will apply a simple pre-filter to speed up the analysis. Genes with fewer than 10 counts in total across all samples provide little information for this comparison, and removing them reduces the size of the dataset. The code uses logical operators and row selection similar to those used to identify zero-count genes in sample h1.1.






NoteYou do not need to memorise this code



For now, focus on what the code does:

calculates the total count for each gene in the dataset
identifies genes with a total count of at least 10
retains those gene rows.

An optional activity later in this session unpacks each operation in more detail.



# Calculate the total count for each gene across all samples
gene_total <- rowSums(counts(dds))

# Identify genes with at least 10 counts in total
keep_gene <- gene_total >= 10

# Retain the selected gene rows and all sample columns
dds_filtered <- dds[keep_gene, ]

The expression used to filter dds follows the familiar indexing pattern:
object[rows, columns]
In this case:

keep_gene appears before the comma, so it selects gene rows
nothing appears after the comma, so all sample columns are retained







TipTry it yourself: Check the result



It is always good practice to check that a statement did what you expected. Run the following code:

dim(dds)

[1] 65217    21

dim(dds_filtered)

[1] 30076    21


Compare the two outputs and answer:

Did the number of genes change?
Did the number of samples change?
Why did filtering affect the rows but not the columns?









TipSolution






The number of genes decreased because genes with fewer than 10 total counts were removed.
The number of samples did not change because the filter was applied to the rows.
keep_gene appears before the comma, so it selects gene rows. Nothing appears after the comma, so all sample columns are retained.

dds_filtered <- dds[keep_gene, ]
For this dataset, the dimensions should change from:
65,217 genes × 21 samples
to:
30,076 genes × 21 samples
Therefore, the filter removes:

nrow(dds) - nrow(dds_filtered)

[1] 35141


This should return 35141.









WarningWhat filtering does and does not mean



This is a simple pre-filter based only on the total number of counts available for each gene.

Passing the filter does not mean that a gene is differentially expressed.
Passing the filter does not mean that a gene is strongly expressed in every sample.
Failing the filter does not mean that a gene has no biological importance.
Filtering does not transform or normalise the retained counts.
Filtering removes complete gene rows but retains all biological samples.

The threshold of 10 is a simple threshold we are using to speed up analysis rather than a universal rule for every RNA-seq analysis.


We will use the new dds_filtered object when fitting the model in the next chapter.

You have now completed the required activities for this chapter. The remaining section is an optional, but valuable challenge for further practice. You can attempt it now or return to it later.






TipOptional Activity 1: Investigate low-count filtering



In the main workflow, we used the following code to remove genes with fewer than 10 counts in total across all samples:

5.10.2 Further challenge: Compare thresholds
Create a vector containing several possible thresholds:

thresholds <- c(0, 1, 10, 20, 50, 100)

Calculate how many genes would be retained at each threshold:

genes_retained <- sapply(
  thresholds,
  function(threshold) {
    sum(gene_total >= threshold)

)

Combine the results into a data frame:

threshold_summary <- data.frame(
  threshold = thresholds,
  genes_retained = genes_retained
)

Calculate the number removed at each threshold:

threshold_summary$genes_removed <-
  nrow(dds) - threshold_summary$genes_retained
