text:
6.2 Fitting the DESeq2 model
We have now prepared a DESeqDataSet called dds_filtered containing:

the original RNA-seq counts
information describing each sample
the design formula ~ status
only genes that passed our low-count filter

The next step is to fit the DESeq2 model:

dds_fitted <- DESeq(dds_filtered)

During this step the DESeq() function performs the main calculations needed to compare gene expression between the biological groups by fitting the model. Although this requires only one line of R code, several steps take place.
Adjust for size differences between sequencing libraries
The total number of reads collected can differ between samples. A sample with a larger sequencing library may therefore have higher counts for many genes, even when there is no biological difference in expression.
DESeq2 estimates a size factor for each sample. These size factors allow the model to account for differences in sequencing depth and library composition when comparing samples.
This does not mean that DESeq2 replaces the original counts with log-transformed values. The model still uses the original integer counts.
Estimate variability among biological samples
Counts for the same gene will not be identical in every person, even when the people belong to the same biological group.
DESeq2 estimates the dispersion of each gene. Dispersion describes how much the counts for that gene vary among biological samples, beyond the variation expected from counting alone.
This is important because an apparent difference between groups is more convincing when the samples within each group show reasonably consistent patterns.
For example, imagine that two genes have the same estimated difference between HAT and SERO TL+:

the first gene has similar counts among the people within each group
the second gene has very different counts among people within the same group

The difference between groups would usually be more convincing for the first gene because there is less variability among its biological replicates.
Estimate differences associated with status
Finally, DESeq2 uses the design formula:
~ status
to fit a separate model for each gene.
The model estimates how the expected count for a gene differs among the levels of status, while accounting for library size and variability among biological samples. These estimated group differences are stored as model coefficients.
At this stage, the model contains information about all three status groups. We have not yet requested the particular HAT-versus-SERO TL+ comparison. We will do that in the next step using results().






NoteA simplified overview



For each gene, DESeq2 broadly asks:

How should differences in sequencing depth between samples be accounted for?
How much do the counts vary among biological samples?
How large is the estimated difference between the biological groups?
Is that difference large relative to its uncertainty?

The final question is assessed using a statistical test. You are not expected to reproduce these calculations yourself.



6.2.1 What is stored in dds_fitted?
The dds_fitted object contains the same filtered counts, sample information and design as dds_filtered, together with information estimated during model fitting, including size factors, dispersions and model coefficients.
It contains the same filtered counts, sample information and design as dds_filtered, together with the information estimated during model fitting, including size factors, dispersions and model coefficients.
We have used a new object name rather than overwriting dds_filtered to make it easier to distinguish between:

dds, containing the original genes
dds_filtered, containing the genes that passed the filter
dds_fitted, containing the filtered data and fitted model

text:
6.3 Extracting the HAT-versus-SERO TL+ contrast
Finally, we will extract our comparison of interest (HAT vs SERO TL+) using a contrast. This tells DESeq2 exactly which two groups to compare and in which direction.

res_hat_vs_sero <- results(
  dds_fitted,
  contrast = c("status", "hat", "sero"),
  alpha = 0.05
)

The three values in contrast = c("status", "hat", "sero") specify:

the metadata variable being compared (status)
the numerator group (hat)
the denominator, or reference, group for this comparison (sero)


6.3.1 Interpreting log2 fold change
DESeq2 reports differences between groups as a log2FoldChange. This is the estimated fold change expressed on a log2 scale.
Using a log2 scale makes increases and decreases easier to compare (similar to how we transformed the counts to make them easier to compare in Chapter 4:

log2FoldChange = 0 means no estimated difference
log2FoldChange = 1 means approximately 2-fold higher expression
log2FoldChange = 2 means approximately 4-fold higher expression
log2FoldChange = -1 means approximately 2-fold lower expression
log2FoldChange = -2 means approximately 4-fold lower expression

The direction always depends on the order of the comparison. For HAT versus SERO TL+:

a positive value indicates higher estimated expression in HAT
a negative value indicates higher estimated expression in SERO TL+







TipTry it yourself: Practice interpreting log2 fold change



For a HAT versus SERO TL+ comparison, what would each result mean?

log2FoldChange = 0
log2FoldChange = 1
log2FoldChange = -1
log2FoldChange = 2









TipSuggested answers






log2FoldChange = 0 means that there is no estimated difference in expression between HAT and SERO TL+.
log2FoldChange = 1 means that estimated expression is approximately 2-fold higher in HAT than in SERO (\(2^1 = 2\)-fold).
log2FoldChange = -1 means that estimated expression is approximately half as high in HAT as in SERO TL+, because (2^{-1} = 0.5). Equivalently, estimated expression is approximately 2-fold higher in SERO TL+ than in HAT.
log2FoldChange = 2 means that estimated expression is approximately 4-fold higher in HAT than in SERO TL+ (\(2^2 = 4\)-fold).










WarningFold change is relative



A log2 fold change describes gene expression in one group relative to another group. It does not tell us the absolute expression of the gene.
For the HAT versus SERO TL+ comparison:

a positive value means estimated expression is higher in HAT
a negative value means estimated expression is higher in SERO TL+
a value of zero means there is no estimated difference between the groups

For example, log2FoldChange = -1 means that estimated expression in HAT is approximately half that in SERO TL+:
\[
2^{-1} = 0.5
\]
The interpretation always depends on the order of the comparison.

Neither value alone establishes biological importance.








WarningInterpreting padj = NA



Some genes have padj = NA because an adjusted p-value was not available. This can occur when a gene contains too little information for reliable testing or when it is excluded from multiple-testing adjustment by DESeq2’s internal procedures.
An NA does not mean that the gene is significantly or non-significantly different. It means that an adjusted result is unavailable.

In Chapter 6, you fitted the DESeq2 model and extracted a HAT-versus-SERO TL+ contrast. We will reload the fitted model and recreate the results table before exploring the gene-level evidence with plots and annotations.

In this session, you’ll explore the HAT-versus-SERO TL+ results in more detail. You’ll use an MA plot to examine how estimated expression differences vary with gene abundance, create a volcano plot that combines effect size with statistical evidence, compare what the two plots show, add gene symbols and investigate IRF8 to develop a cautious biological interpretation.

ISCB alignment: A3 (interpret candidate genes in their molecular and immunological context), C3 (combine statistical, visual and biological evidence to generate cautious hypotheses), D3 (construct and compare MA and volcano plots and apply explicit prioritisation thresholds), E3 (retain stable identifiers and add traceable gene annotations), F3 (use appropriate plotting and annotation resources), H3 (create derived variables, layered plots and guided identifier matches in R), K3 (communicate effect size, statistical evidence and biological relevance separately).








TipTry it yourself: Discuss the data



Discuss these questions with a partner before running any code to refresh what you did in the last session:

What did each row of the count matrix represent?
What did each column represent?
What did the design ~ status tell DESeq2?
In the contrast HAT versus SERO TL+, what does a positive log2FoldChange mean?
Why is padj more useful than an unadjusted p-value when thousands of genes are tested?
Does a statistically significant result necessarily represent a large or biologically important difference?









TipSolution






Each row represented one gene. The values across each row were the read counts assigned to that specific gene in each sample.
Each column represented one biological sample. The column contained the read counts for all genes measured in that sample.
The design ~ status told DESeq2 to model gene expression using the status variable. In this analysis, status distinguishes samples classified as HAT from those classified as SERO TL+.
A positive log2FoldChange means that the gene had higher estimated expression in HAT versus SERO TL+. A negative value means higher estimated expression in SERO TL+.
padj is a p-value adjusted to account for multiple testing. When thousands of genes are tested, some small unadjusted p-values will occur by chance. Using adjusted p-values reduces the risk of drawing false-positive conclusions.
No, statistical significance does not necessarily mean that a difference is large or biologically important. A gene can have a small fold change but strong statistical evidence, particularly when the measurements are consistent. Biological importance must be evaluated using the effect size, expression abundance, biological context, study design and any other supporting evidence.

section: 7.3 Examine how expression differences vary with gene abundance
text:
7.3 Examine how expression differences vary with gene abundance
First, we want to examine how the estimated expression differences between HAT and SERO TL+ vary with gene abundance. This is important because a large fold change is not equally convincing at every level of abundance. When a gene has very few counts, small differences in the observed counts can produce a large estimated fold change and that estimate may be relatively uncertain. Genes with higher counts usually provide more information, allowing their fold changes to be estimated more precisely.
An MA plot allows us to examine gene abundance and estimated expression differences together. It provides an overview of the differential expression result for all tested genes, with each point representing one gene.
The term MA plot refers to the two quantities traditionally shown:

M represents the log ratio between two measurements. Here, it will be the estimated log2FoldChange for HAT compared with SERO TL+.
A represents average abundance. Here, it is represented by the mean normalised count, or baseMean.

The plot shows:

Horizontal position: the mean normalised expression of the gene across all samples, displayed on a logarithmic scale.
Vertical position: the estimated log2 fold change for HAT compared with SERO TL+.
Colour: whether the adjusted p-value is below the value supplied to alpha.

Genes with low mean counts appear on the left, while genes with high mean counts appear on the right. Genes above zero have higher estimated expression in HAT, while genes below zero have higher estimated expression in SERO TL+.
If most genes do not differ strongly between the groups, the main cloud of points should be centred approximately around a log2 fold change of zero. The vertical spread is often wider on the left because fold changes are less precisely estimated for genes with low counts. Toward the right, the greater amount of count information usually produces more stable estimates, so the points often form a narrower band around zero.
The MA plot therefore helps us ask whether large estimated differences occur mainly among low-abundance genes, whether changes occur in both directions, and whether there are broader patterns across the range of gene abundances. A large fold change may be interesting but it should be considered alongside abundance, uncertainty and statistical evidence.
We can create an MA plot from the DESeq2 result using the plotMA() function. The function uses an adjusted p-value threshold of 0.1 by default. We will explicitly use alpha = 0.05 so that the threshold is consistent with the other analyses we will do that use a p-value threshold of 0.05.

plotMA(
  res_hat_vs_sero,
  alpha = 0.05,
  main = "MA plot: HAT versus SERO TL+"
)









7.3.1 What does the MA plot tell us?
We use the MA plot to check whether the estimated fold changes appear reasonable across the range of gene abundances. In particular, we want to know whether large fold changes occur mainly among low-count genes, where the estimates are generally less precise.
Examine the plot and discuss the following questions with a partner before revealing the solution:

Is the main cloud of genes centred approximately around a log2FoldChange of zero?
Is the spread of fold changes wider among genes with low or high mean counts?
Are genes with padj < 0.05 found above and below zero?
Based on the plot, which fold changes should be interpreted most cautiously and why?







TipSolution






Yes. The main cloud is centred approximately around zero, indicating that many genes have relatively small estimated expression differences between HAT and SERO TL+.
The spread is widest among genes with low mean counts and generally becomes narrower as abundance increases. This is because low-count genes provide less information for estimating fold changes.
Yes. Blue points occur above and below zero. The result therefore includes genes with adjusted p-values below 0.05 that have higher estimated expression in HAT and genes that have higher estimated expression in SERO TL+.
Large fold changes among genes with low mean counts should be interpreted most cautiously. Small differences in low counts can produce large fold-change estimates, and these estimates are generally less precise. Fold-change size should therefore be considered alongside abundance and statistical evidence.

Overall, the plot suggests that many genes have relatively small estimated differences, while subsets of genes differ in both directions. Many of the most extreme fold changes occur among low-abundance genes, so a large fold change alone is not sufficient evidence that a gene is biologically important.









WarningWhat if the MA plot looks unusual?



An MA plot does not need to form a perfect funnel or be exactly symmetrical. Real biological differences may produce more changes in one direction than the other.
However, some patterns should prompt further investigation:

Most points are shifted above or below zero: there may be a widespread biological difference, a change in cell composition or a problem with normalisation, sample labels or the model design.
There is a curve or trend across the abundance range: the estimated fold changes may depend systematically on gene abundance.
The spread remains very wide among high-abundance genes: some samples may be unusually variable or influential.
Almost all large fold changes occur among very low-abundance genes: the apparent differences may be driven mainly by uncertain estimates based on small counts.

An unusual MA plot does not identify the cause or automatically mean that the analysis has failed. It tells us we need to examine the sample metadata, count distributions, model design and sample-level plots before drawing biological conclusions.




7.3.2 Saving the MA plot
When we used ggplot2 previously, we could store a plot in an R object and save that object using ggsave(). The plotMA() function works differently. It draws the plot directly rather than returning a ggplot2 object so we will have to save it using the base R graphics system.
Saving a base R plot involves three steps:

Use png() to open a PNG graphics device and specify the output filename.
Run the plotting code. While the graphics device is open, the plot is sent to the PNG file instead of being displayed in the Plots pane.
Use dev.off() to close the graphics device and finish writing the image file.


png(
  filename = "figures/MA_hat_vs_sero.png"
)
plotMA(
  res_hat_vs_sero,
  alpha = 0.05,
  main = "MA plot: HAT versus SERO TL+"
)
dev.off()

section: 7.4 Examine effect size and statistical evidence together
text:
7.4 Examine effect size and statistical evidence together
The MA plot helped us examine whether estimated fold changes varied with gene abundance. We will now consider a different question: which genes combine a relatively large estimated expression difference with strong statistical evidence?
These genes may be useful candidates for further biological investigation. However, a large, statistically supported difference does not automatically make a gene biologically important.
A volcano plot shows:

Horizontal position: the estimated log2FoldChange for HAT compared with SERO TL+.
Vertical position: the adjusted p-value after a -log10 transformation.
Colour: whether a gene passes the selected fold-change and adjusted p-value thresholds.

Genes with negative fold changes appear on the left and have higher estimated expression in SERO TL+. Genes with positive fold changes appear on the right and have higher estimated expression in HAT.
Genes with smaller adjusted p-values appear higher on the plot. Therefore, genes that combine larger fold changes with stronger statistical evidence appear toward the upper-left or upper-right.
Unlike the MA plot, a volcano plot does not show gene abundance. The two plots answer different questions and should be interpreted together.

7.4.1 Prepare the data
The vertical axis of a volcano plot typically uses -log10(padj). This transformation makes small adjusted p-values easier to see because smaller values appear higher on the plot. Look back at Chapter 4 for a reminder about logarithmic transformations.
Before applying the transformation, we need to deal with a specific issue. If DESeq2 cannot provide an adjusted p-value for a gene, it records padj = NA. This represents missing information rather than a numerical value, so it cannot be transformed or plotted on an axis. This represents missing information rather than a numerical value and it cannot be transformed or plotted on an axis. We can filter these from the results data frame using the is.na() function using logical row selection, just as we did during low-count filtering in Chapter 5. This function returns TRUE when the value is missing and FALSE when it is present. The symbol ! means not. It reverses the logical values:

!TRUE becomes FALSE
!FALSE becomes TRUE

Therefore, !is.na(result_data$padj) identifies rows where padj is not missing. We can use this statement to remove rows from the result_data data frame with no padj value and create a new data frame called plot_de.

plot_de <- result_data[
  !is.na(result_data$padj),
]

We can now calculate -log10(padj). The negative sign ensures that smaller adjusted p-values produce larger positive values, so genes with stronger statistical evidence appear higher on the plot:

plot_de$minus_log10_padj <- -log10(plot_de$padj)



7.4.2 Highlight genes that pass both thresholds
For this plot, we will highlight genes that have:

an adjusted p-value below 0.05
an absolute log2FoldChange greater than 1. Values greater than 1 indicate more than twofold higher estimated expression in HAT, while values below -1 indicate more than twofold higher estimated expressio in SERO TL+.

In earlier chapters, you created groups by splitting a table into separate parts and then combining those parts again. Here, we will use a shorter approach.






NoteYou do not need to memorise this code



For now, focus on what the code does.
We will create one new column called direction. Every gene will start in the "Below thresholds" category. We will then replace that value for genes that meet both the adjusted p-value and fold-change conditions.
This keeps all genes in one data frame and gives ggplot2 a single column that it can use to assign colours.

# Start with all genes below the combined thresholds
plot_de$direction <- "Below thresholds"

# Genes higher in HAT
plot_de$direction[
  plot_de$padj < 0.05 &
    plot_de$log2FoldChange > 1
] <- "Higher in HAT"

# Genes higher in SERO TL+
plot_de$direction[
  plot_de$padj < 0.05 &
    plot_de$log2FoldChange < -1
] <- "Higher in SERO TL+"

table(plot_de$direction)


  Below thresholds      Higher in HAT Higher in SERO TL+ 
             21772                395                258 


Genes classified as "Below thresholds" may still have a small adjusted p-value or a large fold change but they do not meet both conditions.
These thresholds help us select genes for further investigation. They do not determine whether a gene is biologically important.




7.4.3 Build the volcano plot using ggplot2
This is the most detailed ggplot2 figure we have created so far. You do not need to memorise all of the code and we will explore ggplot2 and plot customisation in more detail in a later tutorial.
For now, focus on how the plot is built by adding layers. Each layer adds a new feature, such as the points, threshold lines or labels. Hopefully, this example will demonstrate the power of the ggplot2 approach and how a complicated figure can be constructed gradually from a series of simpler components.
Layer 1: Map the data and draw the points
We first specify the data and map three variables to visual features, drawing the genes as points with geom_point:

log2FoldChange will be shown on the x-axis
minus_log10_padj will be shown on the y-axis
direction controls point colour (remember, it will either be Higher in HAT, Higher in SERO TL+ or Below thresholds)


volcano_plot <- ggplot(
  plot_de,
  aes(
    x = log2FoldChange,
    y = minus_log10_padj,
    colour = direction
  )
) +
  geom_point()

volcano_plot














TipTry it yourself: Check the first layer



Before continuing, check that:

negative fold changes appear on the left
positive fold changes appear on the right
smaller adjusted p-values appear higher
the point colours correspond to the categories in direction



Layer 2: Add the threshold lines
We can continue adding layers to the volcano_plot object we have created to build it up. For example, we can add vertical lines for the fold-change thresholds at -1 and 1 using geom_vline(). We also add a horizontal line for the adjusted p-value threshold using geom_hline(). Remember: the value 0.05 must first be transformed because the vertical axis also uses -log10().

volcano_plot <- volcano_plot +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = c(-1, 1),
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey50"
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = -log10(0.05),
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey50"
  )

volcano_plot








Layer 3: Add informative labels
Finally, we add a title, axis labels and a label for the colour legend.

volcano_plot <- volcano_plot +
  labs(
    title = "Volcano plot: HAT versus SERO TL+",
    x = "Log2 fold change: HAT versus SERO TL+",
    y = "-log10 adjusted p-value",
    colour = "Result category"
  )

volcano_plot










7.4.4 What does the volcano plot tell us?
We use the volcano plot to find genes that combine a relatively large estimated expression difference with strong statistical evidence.
Examine the plot and discuss these questions with a partner before revealing the solution:

Is the main cloud of genes centred approximately around a log2FoldChange of zero?
Are genes that pass both thresholds present on the left and right sides of the plot?
What do points in the upper-left and upper-right regions represent?
Which genes might you prioritise for further investigation, and what additional information would you need before judging their biological importance?







TipSolution






The densest part of the main cloud is centred approximately around a log2FoldChange of zero. However, the distribution is not perfectly symmetrical. More genes extend into the positive side of the plot, indicating more substantial expression differences in the HAT direction.
Genes that pass both thresholds are present on both sides of the plot, but they are not equally distributed. There are more green points on the right than blue points on the left. This suggests that more genes pass the selected thresholds with higher estimated expression in HAT than in SERO TL+.
Points in the upper-right have positive fold changes and very small adjusted p-values. These genes have higher estimated expression in HAT and strong statistical evidence for a difference. Points in the upper-left have negative fold changes and small adjusted p-values. These genes have higher estimated expression in SERO TL+ and strong statistical evidence for a difference.
Genes toward the upper-left and upper-right may be useful candidates for further investigation because they combine relatively large fold changes with strong statistical evidence. In this plot, several of the strongest candidates are in the upper-right region. Before judging their biological importance, we would also need to examine their expression abundance, fold-change uncertainty, gene identity, biological function and relevance to HAT.

Overall, the volcano plot shows statistically supported expression differences in both directions, but the result is weighted toward genes with higher estimated expression in HAT. The plot helps us identify candidate genes for further investigation, but it does not show gene abundance or establish biological importance. We therefore need to consider the volcano plot alongside the MA plot and add gene annotations before interpreting particular genes.



The volcano plot highlights candidate genes, but they still need to be identified and interpreted in their biological context.
Does the overall pattern in the volcano plot support a broader biological interpretation, or do we need more information before making one?


7.4.5 Saving the volcano plot
The volcano plot currently only exists as an object in the R Environment. To use the plot outside R, we can save it as an image using the ggsave() function. Try to recall the code from Chapter 3 and Chapter 4 to save the volcano_plot as volcano_hat_vs_sero.png into the figures output directory.






TipSolution






ggsave(
  filename = "figures/volcano_hat_vs_sero.png",
  plot = volcano_plot
)

Saving 7 x 5 in image











WarningWhat can a volcano plot hide?



A volcano plot does not show gene abundance. A gene with a large fold change may have very low counts and a relatively uncertain effect-size estimate.
The upper-left and upper-right points may be useful candidates, but their positions do not prove biological importance. Interpretation also requires the MA plot, the results table, gene annotations and biological context.

match() returns positions rather than symbols. We can use those positions to retrieve the corresponding values from another column, effectively using the annotation data frame as a lookup table.





7.6.3 Match the real gene identifiers
Let’s try it on the Ensembl IDs in the gene_id column of result_data to find which row in annotation_data matches in the ENSEMBL column. We’ll store the vector in a new object called matched_rows.

matched_rows <- match(
  result_data$gene_id,
  annotation_data$ENSEMBL
)

Each value in matched_rows gives the position of that gene in annotation_data. The order of matched_rows follows the order of the genes in result_data.
We can use those row positions to retrieve the equivalent gene symbols in the SYMBOL column of annotation_data and store them as a new column called symbol in result_data:

result_data$symbol <- annotation_data$SYMBOL[
  matched_rows
]

title: 7  Exploring and Annotating Gene-Level Results
text:
7.7 Investigate IRF8
In an earlier tutorial, you found that an immune-related gene had higher expression in HAT. You also know that individuals in the HAT group have overt symptoms, while individuals classified as SERO TL+ do not.
Does the overall pattern in the volcano plot support a broader biological interpretation, or do we need more information before making one?






TipTry it yourself: Investigate a differentially expressed gene



Use the annotated results table to find the row containing the following Ensembl gene identifier:
ENSG00000140968
Use the information in the results table and an appropriate gene database to answer the following questions:

What is the gene symbol associated with this Ensembl identifier?
What is the main biological function of this gene?
What is its log2FoldChange?
Is its estimated expression higher in HAT or SERO TL+?
Convert the log2 fold change into an ordinary fold change using: 2^VALUE
What does the adjusted p-value indicate about the statistical evidence for a difference between the groups?
Based on the function of this gene, suggest why its expression might differ between HAT and SERO TL+ samples.
What additional information or evidence would you need before making a strong biological conclusion?

Write a two- or three-sentence interpretation of the result (you could add it as a comment in your script to remind yourself).








TipPossible Answer






The Ensembl identifier ENSG00000140968 corresponds to Interferon regulatory factor 8 (IRF8), also known as interferon consensus sequence-binding protein.
IRF8 is a transcription factor involved in immune-cell development, particularly in myeloid and lymphoid lineages, and in regulating immune responses to infection.
IRF8 has a log2FoldChange of approximately 1.58.
Because this value is positive for the HAT versus SERO TL+ comparison, its estimated expression is higher in HAT.
Converting the log2 fold change into an ordinary fold change gives:


2^1.58

[1] 2.989698


Estimated IRF8 expression is therefore approximately three times as high in HAT as in SERO TL+.

The adjusted p-value is approximately (2.578 ^{-26}). This provides very strong statistical evidence that IRF8 expression differs between the groups.
IRF8 is a transcription factor involved in immune-cell development and responses to infection. Its higher expression in the HAT samples could therefore be associated with differences in immune activity between the groups.
The result is an association and does not show what caused the difference. It could reflect a change in gene expression within particular cells, differences in the proportions of immune-cell types or other biological or technical differences between the groups.

title: 7  Exploring and Annotating Gene-Level Results
text:
7.8 Bring the results together
So far, we have examined the same differential expression result in three different ways:

the MA plot showed how estimated fold changes varied with gene abundance
the volcano plot showed which genes combined larger estimated differences with stronger statistical evidence
the annotation table allowed us to connect Ensembl identifiers to recognisable gene symbols

Together, these approaches help us move from a large statistical results table toward a possible biological interpretation.






TipTry it yourself: Interpret the data so far



With a partner, select a few annotated genes that you find interesting and discuss:
What overall biological interpretation, if any, is supported by the MA plot, volcano plot and selected genes? What can these results not yet tell us?
You do not need to reach a definitive conclusion. Be prepared to explain which evidence supports your interpretation and what remains uncertain.








TipPossible solution





A reasonable discussion might identify that:

many genes have relatively small estimated differences between HAT and SERO TL+
subsets of genes show larger, statistically supported differences in both directions
more genes pass the selected thresholds with higher estimated expression in HAT than in SERO TL+
some annotated genes may suggest related biological functions, but this depends on which genes are selected
large fold changes among low-abundance genes should be treated cautiously
passing the selected thresholds does not automatically make a gene biologically important

The results support an association between expression and sample status in this dataset. They do not establish that the expression differences caused the symptoms, identify the cell types responsible, or show whether every sample follows the same overall pattern.
It is also reasonable to conclude that more information is needed before proposing a clear biological interpretation.



In the next chapter, the unit of analysis changes. In this session, each plotted point represented a gene. Next time, each plotted point will represent a sample, allowing us to ask whether the overall expression profiles of HAT and SERO TL+ samples show a corresponding global pattern.

title: 7  Exploring and Annotating Gene-Level Results
text:
7.10 Optional extra activities
You have now completed the required activities for this session. The remaining section is an optional, but valuable challenge for further practice. You can attempt it now or return to it later.






TipOptional Activity 1: Choose your own thresholds



The thresholds used in the volcano plot are analytical choices rather than universal rules. Different thresholds may be appropriate depending on the purpose of the analysis.
Independently choose:

an adjusted p-value threshold
a positive and negative log2FoldChange threshold

Modify the classification and plotting code so that the point colours and dashed lines represent your chosen values.
Then answer the following questions:

Why did you choose these thresholds?
How many genes are placed in each category?
How does your plot differ from the original plot?
Did any points move, or did only their categories and colours change?
What are the advantages and disadvantages of your threshold choices?
Which genes might your thresholds exclude from further investigation?
Would you use the same thresholds for every biological question?

Compare your plot and reasoning with a neighbour. If you selected different thresholds, discuss which choice would be most appropriate for selecting a manageable set of genes for further investigation.








TipPossible solution





There is no single correct pair of thresholds. A good response should explain how the chosen thresholds balance effect size, statistical evidence and the purpose of the analysis.
A lower adjusted p-value threshold, such as 0.01, requires stronger statistical evidence. This will usually highlight fewer genes and may produce a more manageable candidate list. However, potentially relevant genes with adjusted p-values between 0.01 and 0.05 will be excluded.
A larger absolute fold-change threshold, such as 1.5, focuses attention on genes with larger estimated differences. However, genes with smaller effects may still be biologically relevant, especially if several genes from the same biological process change together.
A less stringent fold-change threshold, such as 0.5, will include genes with moderate estimated differences. This may help identify coordinated biological patterns, but it may also produce a long candidate list that is difficult to investigate.
The positions of the points should not change because the coordinates are determined by the original log2FoldChange and padj values.
Changing the thresholds should alter the dashed lines and the categories assigned to some genes.
The thresholds should be chosen with reference to the biological question and the planned next step. For example, stricter thresholds might be useful when selecting a small number of genes for experimental validation. Less stringent thresholds might be appropriate when looking for coordinated patterns across pathways or groups of genes.
A strong answer should also recognise that threshold-based selection creates a sharp boundary. Two genes on opposite sides of a threshold may have very similar results. Thresholds are therefore useful for organising and prioritising results, but they should not be treated as a definitive boundary between biologically important and unimportant genes.

title: 8  Exploring Relationships Among Samples
text:
8.1 What you’ll learn
In Chapter 7, we used MA and volcano plots to examine gene-level evidence and added gene symbols so that the results could be interpreted biologically. We are now going to ask a different but complementary question:
Do samples with the same biological status have similar overall expression profiles, and are any samples unusual?
In the MA and volcano plots, each data point represented a gene. In this session, each point will represent a sample. To do this, we will use a few commonly applied methods methods for examining sample relationships, including a principal component analysis (PCA) and a sample-distance heatmap.

8.2 Continue from the previous chapters
Chapter 7 explored gene-level results from the fitted model. In this session, we will reload the model saved in Chapter 6 and derive the sample metadata from it so this session can run after restarting R.

library(DESeq2)
library(ggplot2)

dds_fitted <- readRDS("objects/dds_fitted.rds")
sample_info <- as.data.frame(colData(dds_fitted))

title: 8  Exploring Relationships Among Samples
text:
8.3 Variance-stabilising transformation
In Chapter 4, we used log2(count + 1) to compress a strongly skewed range of count values. However, genes with larger RNA-seq counts also tend to show greater numerical variation among samples. This can cause high-count genes to dominate comparisons between samples.
DESeq2 provides a transformation designed for this purpose called the variance-stabilising transformation, or VST. VST reduces the relationship between a gene’s average expression and its variability, while accounting for differences in sequencing depth. You do not need to understand the mathematical details here. The important idea is that VST values are more suitable for exploratory comparisons among samples, including PCA and sample-distance heatmaps.
As with the earlier log2 transformation, VST values are used for exploratory analysis and visualisation. The differential-expression model continues to use the original count data.
We can transform the count data in our dds_fitted object with the vst() function and store the data in a new object called vsd:

vsd <- vst(dds_fitted, blind = FALSE)







WarningWhy use blind = FALSE?



blind = FALSE allows the transformation to use the fitted experimental design when estimating the mean–variance relationship. This is appropriate here because the design is already known and we are transforming the data for downstream exploration.
The group labels do not directly determine the PCA coordinates or force the samples apart.


It is worth checking that the transformed vsd object and sample_info contain the same sample identifiers in the same order. We can use the identical() function to check whether the sample names in vsd and sample_info are exactly the same and in the same order. Try this without looking back first. If you get stuck, open the solution.
Hint: The sample names are the column names of vsd and the row names of sample_info.






TipSuggested answer





identical(
  colnames(vsd),
  rownames(sample_info)
)
This should return TRUE, confirming that the transformed values and sample information use the same samples in the same order.

section: 8.4 Select HAT and SERO TL+ samples
text:
8.4 Select HAT and SERO TL+ samples
During our analysis, we are focusing on the HAT vs SERO TL+ comparison so we will need to select samples from those groups from the vsd. We can use the information in sample_info to obtain the names of samples in the groups we want:

selected_samples <- rownames(sample_info)[
  sample_info$status == "sero" | sample_info$status == "hat"
]

selected_samples

 [1] "h1.1"  "h1.2"  "h1.3"  "h1.5"  "h2.2"  "h2.3"  "h2.4"  "h2.5"  "h2.6" 
[10] "shi.1" "shi.2" "slo.1" "slo.5" "slo.6" "slo.7"


In this statement, R asks two questions for each sample:

Is the sample’s status "sero"?
Is the sample’s status "hat"?

The | symbol means OR, so only one of these questions needs to have the answer TRUE.
A sample is therefore selected if its status is "sero" or "hat". Samples with any other status are not selected. Finally, the square brackets use these TRUE and FALSE results to keep the names of the selected samples. Make sure that all the samples marked as HAT or SERO TL+ in the data are in the new vector.

all(selected_samples %in% colnames(vsd))

[1] TRUE


The check should return TRUE. We can select the columns directly by their sample names:

selected_vsd <- vsd[, selected_samples]

It is worth verifying the data after subsetting to make sure nothing has gone wrong. For example, We can use dim() to report the numbers of rows and columns, colnames() to display the sample names, and table() to summarise the status variable:

ctrl  hat sero

title: 8  Exploring Relationships Among Samples
text:
8.6 Calculate the PCA
A PCA summarises the major patterns of variation across many genes. We will use DESeq2’s plotPCA() function to prepare the PCA data that we will plot with ggplot2:

each point represents one sample
samples with more similar expression profiles appear closer together
samples with less similar expression profiles appear farther apart

We will store the PCA in a new object called pca_data:

pca_data <- plotPCA(
  selected_vsd,
  intgroup = "status",
  ntop = 500,
  returnData = TRUE
)

using ntop=500 top features by variance



selected_vsd specifies the variance-stabilised expression data for the selected samples.
intgroup = "status" retrieves the status for each sample so that this meta-information can be used when plotting the PCA
returnData = TRUE tells plotPCA() to return the PCA coordinates and sample information as a data frame rather than drawing it immediately
ntop = 500 tells plotPCA() to calculate the PCA using the 500 genes with the greatest variation across the selected samples

Genes that barely vary across the samples provide little information about how the samples differ. plotPCA() therefore focuses on the genes that vary most across the selected samples, often the 500 most variable genes. The number 500 is a practical default rather than a strict biological rule. It includes enough genes to represent broad expression patterns while reducing the influence of thousands of genes that change very little.
The returned data frame contains one row for each sample:

PC1 gives the horizontal coordinate of each sample
PC2 gives the vertical coordinate of each sample
group contains the sample status
name contains the sample identifier

title: 8  Exploring Relationships Among Samples
text:
8.7 Plot the PCA
We now have everything we need to plot the PCA using ggplot2.






TipTry it yourself: Create the PCA plot



Previously, we have built plots using this general structure:
a_plot <- ggplot(
  data = a_data_frame,
  mapping = aes(
    x = an_x_variable,
    y = a_y_variable
  )
) +
  a_geom()
We will reuse that structure with geom_point(), similar to the volcano plot in Chapter 7. Complete the code and then run it by replacing the blanks with the names below. Try this without looking back first. If you get stuck, open the suggested answers

pca_data
PC1
PC2
group

Remember:

the first argument to ggplot() is the data frame
x controls horizontal position
y controls vertical position
colour identifies the sample groups

pca_plot <- ggplot(
  ___________________,
  aes(
    x = __________,
    y = __________,
    colour = __________
  )
) +
  geom_point()

pca_plot








TipSuggested answer






pca_plot <- ggplot(
  pca_data,
  aes(
    x = PC1,
    y = PC2,
    colour = group
  )
) +
  geom_point()

pca_plot











The PCA plot shows the samples along the first two principal components, PC1 and PC2.
The percentage for each axis tells us how much of the overall variation among samples is represented by that principal component. This helps us judge how much of the dataset is summarised by the plot.
We can extract these percentages so that we can include them in the axis labels using an additional ggplot2 layer (you do not need to memorise all of the code):

# Calculate the percentage variation represented by PC1 and PC2
pc1_percent <- round(
  100 * attr(pca_data, "percentVar")[1],
  1
)

pc2_percent <- round(
  100 * attr(pca_data, "percentVar")[2],
  1
)

#add them to the pca plot
pca_plot <- pca_plot +
  labs(
    x = paste0("PC1 (", pc1_percent, "%)"),
    y = paste0("PC2 (", pc2_percent, "%)")
  )

pca_plot














TipTry it yourself: Interpret the PCA plot



Examine the plot and discuss these questions with a partner before revealing the suggested answers:
Read the plot

What does each point represent?
How much variation is represented by PC1 and PC2 individually?
How much variation do PC1 and PC2 represent together?

Describe the pattern

Along which axis are the HAT and SERO TL+ samples separated most clearly?
Is the separation between the two groups complete, partial or absent?
Is there still variation among samples belonging to the same group?

Interpret the biology

What does the separation suggest about the relationship between sample status and overall gene expression?
Does PC1 representing 27.2% mean that disease status explains exactly 27.2% of the variation? Explain your answer.

Complete the interpretation below (you could add it as a comment in your script to remind yourself):
# PC1 represents _____% of the variation among the samples. The separation along PC1 suggests that __________. However, __________.








TipSuggested answers






Each point represents one biological sample. The position of each point summarises the expression values of the 500 most variable genes in that sample.
PC1 represents 27.2%, while PC2 represents 17.4%, of the variation among the samples.
Together, PC1 and PC2 represent:
27.2% + 17.4% = 44.6%
The remaining variation is represented by other principal components that are not shown in this plot.
The HAT and SERO TL+ samples are separated most clearly along PC1, the horizontal axis.
The groups do not overlap along PC1 in this displayed two-dimensional projection. All HAT samples have negative PC1 values, while all SERO TL+ samples have positive PC1 values.
Yes. Samples within each group have different positions, particularly along PC2. This shows that samples belonging to the same status group do not have identical expression profiles.
The separation suggests that sample status is associated with an important pattern in overall gene expression. This is consistent with HAT and SERO TL+ samples having different expression profiles across many genes.
No. PC1 captures 27.2% of all the variation represented by these genes but the PCA does not tell us how much of that variation was caused by disease status. Disease status is associated with position along PC1 but other biological or technical factors could also contribute to the same axis.

A possible interpretation is:
# PC1 represents 27.2% of the variation among the samples. HAT and SERO TL+ samples do not overlap along PC1 in the displayed PCA, suggests that status is associated with an important pattern in overall gene expression. However, the PCA does not demonstrate that disease status caused the pattern, and other biological or technical factors may also contribute to the variation.

title: 8  Exploring Relationships Among Samples
text:
8.9 Examine distances between samples
PCA compresses the variation among samples into a small number of axes. This makes broad patterns easier to see but a two-dimensional PCA plot does not display all the variation in the data. A sample-distance matrix can provide a complementary view by comparing samples across all the VST-transformed genes:

a smaller distance means that two samples have more similar expression profiles
a larger distance means that two samples have less similar expression profiles
the distance between a sample and itself is zero

This allows us to examine individual sample pairs and ask whether samples from the same status group are generally more similar to one another. It can also help identify samples that differ from the other members of their group that may need to be investigated in more detail.
We can use dist() function to calculate the distances between samples and then compare the result with the pattern observed in the PCA.
Prepare the values for the distance calculation
For the PCA, we created selected_vsd, which contains the transformed expression values and sample information for the HAT and SERO TL+ samples. However, dist() requires a numeric matrix. We must therefore extract the transformed expression values using the assay() accessor:

selected_vst <- assay(selected_vsd)

selected_vst contains just the transformed expression values in a matrix. Unlike selected_vsd, there is no sample information.

each row represents one gene
each column represents one sample

However, dist() calculates distances between rows. We want to compare samples, so samples must be in rows and genes must be in columns. We therefore transpose the matrix using the t() function:

sample_by_gene <- t(selected_vst)

We can now calculate the distance between each sample and every other sample. The dist() function stores its result in a specialised compact format, so we use as.matrix() to convert it into a standard matrix containing the distance for every pair of samples:

sample_dist_matrix <- as.matrix(
  dist(sample_by_gene)
)

sample_dist_matrix[1:5, 1:5]

         h1.1     h1.2     h1.3     h1.5     h2.2
h1.1  0.00000 74.00000 71.22884 75.22306 81.09497
h1.2 74.00000  0.00000 81.19974 85.40769 86.75288
h1.3 71.22884 81.19974  0.00000 74.79282 79.87624
h1.5 75.22306 85.40769 74.79282  0.00000 87.46169
h2.2 81.09497 86.75288 79.87624 87.46169  0.00000


By default, dist() uses Euclidean distance. This combines the differences across all genes into one distance value for each pair of samples. You do not need to calculate this by hand.
In the resulting matrix:

each cell contains the distance between two samples
smaller values indicate more similar expression profiles
larger values indicate less similar expression profiles
the diagonal is zero because each sample is identical to itself
the matrix is symmetrical because the distance from sample A to sample B is the same as the distance from sample B to sample A.

Prepare the distances for plotting
In Chapter 3, we used stack() to reshape a wide format gene-count matrix into a long format data frame for ggplot(). The same principle applies here, but each distance is associated with two sample names

the sample named by the matrix row
the sample named by the matrix column

Instead of stack(), we use as.table() because it collects the matrix cells into rows while retaining both sample names:

distance_data <- as.data.frame(
  as.table(sample_dist_matrix)
)

head(distance_data)

  Var1 Var2     Freq
1 h1.1 h1.1  0.00000
2 h1.2 h1.1 74.00000
3 h1.3 h1.1 71.22884
4 h1.5 h1.1 75.22306
5 h2.2 h1.1 81.09497
6 h2.3 h1.1 76.75551


The resulting data frame initially has three columns:

Var1: the sample from the matrix row
Var2: the sample from the matrix column
Freq: the distance between those samples

Just like after stack(), these names are not very informative so we will replace them:

colnames(distance_data) <- c(
  "sample_1",
  "sample_2",
  "distance"
)

head(distance_data)

  sample_1 sample_2 distance
1     h1.1     h1.1  0.00000
2     h1.2     h1.1 74.00000
3     h1.3     h1.1 71.22884
4     h1.5     h1.1 75.22306
5     h2.2     h1.1 81.09497
6     h2.3     h1.1 76.75551


Each row of distance_data now represents one pair of samples and contains the distance between their transformed expression profiles.






TipTry it yourself: Interpret the distance data



Examine the first few rows of distance_data and answer these questions before revealing the suggested answers:

What does one row represent?
Which columns identify the two samples being compared?
Which column contains the distance between them?
What would a relatively small distance mean?









TipSuggested answers






One row represents one comparison between a pair of samples.
sample_1 and sample_2 identify the two samples being compared. These were the row and column names in the original distance matrix.
distance contains the calculated distance between their transformed expression profiles.
A relatively small distance means that the two samples have more similar expression profiles across the VST-transformed genes retained in `selected_vsd.

title: 8  Exploring Relationships Among Samples
section: 8.10 Display the sample distances as a heatmap
text:
8.10 Display the sample distances as a heatmap
The distance matrix contains all the pairwise sample comparisons, but a large table of numbers is difficult for us to interpret. A heatmap displays the same values using colour and makes broader patterns easier to identify.
We can use the heatmap to look for:

groups of samples with relatively small distances
samples with relatively large distances
whether samples from the same status group tend to have similar expression profiles
samples that differ from the other members of their group

The heatmap does not calculate any new distances. It is just a visual representation of the distances we have already calculated.
For previous ggplot2 figures, we used several different functions to plot different graphs, such as geom_point() and geom_boxplot(). For a heatmap, we use geom_tile() to draw a rectangular tile for every row of distance_data.
For this plot:

x identifies the first sample
y identifies the second sample
fill controls the colour of the tile
each tile represents the distance between one pair of samples







TipTry it yourself: Re-arrange the heatmap code



The lines below are in the wrong order. Before revealing the solution, try and rearrange them to create a heatmap in which:

sample_1 is displayed on the horizontal axis
sample_2 is displayed on the vertical axis

TipTry it yourself: Interpret the heatmap



Examine the heatmap and discuss these questions with a partner before revealing the suggested answers:

Why are the tiles along the diagonal dark purple?
Do the HAT samples appear to have similar expression profiles to one another?
Do the SERO TL+ samples form an equally consistent group?
How do the distances between HAT and SERO TL+ samples compare with the distances among the HAT samples?
Does the heatmap support the overall pattern seen in the PCA?
What can the heatmap not tell us about the cause of the pattern?

Complete the interpretation below (you could add it as a comment in your script to remind yourself):
# The distance heatmap shows that __________. This supports the PCA because __________. However, __________.








TipSuggested answers






The diagonal compares each sample with itself. A sample has a distance of zero from itself, so these tiles have the darkest colour.
The HAT samples form a relatively consistent block of smaller distances. This suggests that the HAT samples have broadly similar expression profiles across the genes used in the calculation.
The distances among the SERO TL+ samples are more variable. Some sample pairs have relatively similar profiles, while others have larger distances. The SERO TL+ samples therefore appear more heterogeneous than the HAT samples.
Distances between HAT and SERO TL+ samples are generally larger than distances among the HAT samples. This is visible from the lighter colours in comparisons between the groups.
Yes. The PCA showed a distinction between the HAT and SERO TL+ samples. The distance heatmap supports this by showing relatively small distances among HAT samples and generally larger distances between the two groups.
The heatmap cannot tell us what caused the pattern. Biological variation, differences in cell composition, clinical characteristics or technical variation could all contribute. These possibilities would need to be investigated using the sample metadata and quality-control information.

A possible interpretation is:
# The distance heatmap shows that the HAT samples have relatively similar expression profiles, while the SERO TL+ samples are more varied. This supports the PCA because both plots show a distinction between the HAT and SERO TL+ expression profiles. However, the heatmap does not explain the greater variation among the SERO TL+ samples.

8.12 Integrate the evidence
We have examined the HAT and SERO TL+ comparison at two levels:

DESeq2, the MA plot and the volcano plot described differences in individual genes.
The PCA and sample-distance heatmap described broader patterns across the samples.

We will now combine this evidence into one biological interpretation.






ImportantTry it yourself: Summarise the data



Use the gene-level figures from Chapter 7 and the sample-level figures created in this chapter to answer the following questions.

8.12.1 Describe the sample-level pattern

How are the HAT and SERO TL+ samples positioned along PC1?
Which group has the more consistent overall expression profiles?
What evidence shows that the SERO TL+ samples are more heterogeneous?



8.12.2 Connect the sample-level and gene-level evidence

How is the separation in the PCA consistent with the differential-expression results from Chapter 7?
What additional information does the distance heatmap provide that is not as clear in the PCA?



8.12.3 Evaluate the biological interpretation

Could the greater variation among SERO TL+ samples be related to variation in their infection or clinical phenotype?
What other biological or technical factors could produce this pattern?
What additional data or analysis would help distinguish among these explanations?

Complete the interpretation below (you could add it as a comment in your script to remind yourself):
# The PCA and distance heatmap show that __________. This is consistent with the gene-level results because __________. The greater variation among the SERO TL+ samples could reflect __________. However, __________ would need to be examined before drawing a causal conclusion.









TipSuggested answers






The HAT and SERO TL+ samples are completely separated along PC1 in the displayed PCA. All HAT samples have negative PC1 values, while all SERO TL+ samples have positive PC1 values.
The HAT samples have the more consistent overall expression profiles. The HAT samples generally have smaller distances from one another in the sample-distance heatmap.
The SERO TL+ samples are spread across PC1 and PC2 in the PCA and have more variable pairwise distances in the heatmap. Some SERO TL+ sample pairs have relatively similar profiles, while other pairs have larger distances.
Chapter 7 identified differences in the expression of many individual genes between HAT and SERO TL+. The separation in the PCA shows that these gene-level differences are accompanied by a broader difference in the overall expression profiles of the samples.
The PCA provides a compressed two-dimensional summary of the major expression patterns. The distance heatmap shows every pairwise sample comparison. It therefore makes the relatively consistent HAT group and the greater heterogeneity among SERO TL+ samples easier to see.
Possibly. SERO TL+ individuals may have less uniform infection or clinical characteristics than individuals with symptomatic HAT. Variation in immune response, infection stage, parasite exposure or progression towards disease could contribute to their different expression profiles. These explanations are hypotheses and are not demonstrated by the plots.
Other explanations include differences in blood-cell composition, age, sex, sample collection, RNA quality, sequencing depth, processing batch or other participant characteristics.
Useful follow-up information could include clinical measurements, symptom severity, parasitological evidence, immune-cell counts, demographic metadata and technical quality-control variables. The expression patterns could then be tested for associations with these variables. Cell-type-specific or single-cell measurements could help distinguish changes within cells from differences in cell composition.

A possible interpretation is:
# The PCA and distance heatmap show that HAT and SERO TL+ samples have distinct overall expression profiles, with the HAT samples forming a relatively consistent group and the SERO TL+ samples showing greater variation. This is consistent with the gene-level results because the previous chapter identified many genes whose expression differed between the two status groups. The greater variation among the SERO TL+ samples could reflect variation in infection, immune response or clinical phenotype. However, clinical metadata, cell composition and possible technical variables would need to be examined before drawing a causal conclusion.









WarningWhat if the sample pattern looks unexpected?



The PCA and the sample-distance heatmap do not need to show perfect separation between HAT and SERO TL+. Samples from the same biological group will not have identical expression profiles and genuine biological variation may exist within each group.
However, some patterns should prompt further investigation:

One or a small number of samples are far from all the others in the PCA: the samples may be biologically unusual, affected by a technical problem or incorrectly labelled.
One sample or a small number of samples have large distances from every other sample in the heatmap: this supports the possibility that these samples are unusual across their overall expression profile.
Samples form subgroups that are not explained by status: another variable, such as batch, sampling location, clinical characteristics or cell composition may be associated with the expression pattern.
Samples separate by a technical variable rather than status: the apparent pattern may be influenced by how or when the samples were processed.
The status groups overlap extensively: status may not be the main source of variation, or the biological difference may affect only a subset of genes rather than the overall expression profile.
PCA and the heatmap appear to disagree: inspect which principal components are displayed, how much variation they explain and whether a small number of samples are influencing the pattern.

An unusual sample should not be removed simply because it looks different. First check the sample metadata, quality-control results, count distributions and experimental records. A sample should only be excluded when there is a clear and documented biological or technical reason.
These plots can show that a pattern requires investigation, but they cannot determine its cause by themselves.

8.14 Optional extra activities
You have now completed the required activities for this chapter. The remaining activities provide optional but valuable opportunities for further practice.






TipOptional Activity 1: Challenge an overclaim



A researcher writes the following using the same results that you have produced so far:
“The HAT and SERO TL+ samples separate in the PCA, so HAT causes the observed gene-expression pattern.”
What is wrong with this conclusion and what can the PCA actually show us?
Use evidence from the following analyses to rewrite the statement:

the MA plot
the volcano plot
the annotated differential-expression results
the PCA
the sample-distance heatmap

Your revised interpretation should:

describe the main gene-level pattern
describe the sample-level pattern shown by both the PCA and sample-distance heatmap
acknowledge variation within the HAT and SERO TL+ groups
propose one possible biological explanation
give at least one alternative biological or technical explanation
explain why the current analysis cannot establish causation
propose a follow-up analysis or measurement that could help distinguish between the explanations

Aim to write one short scientific paragraph rather than answering each point separately.
Before writing, consider the difference between:

observation: something shown directly by the analysis
interpretation: a possible explanation for the observation
conclusion: a claim that is justified by the available evidence









TipPossible solution





The study compares existing groups rather than experimentally assigning sample status. Separation in a PCA shows that an expression pattern is associated with the groups, but PCA does not determine the cause of that pattern.
In addition, PC1 and PC2 display only part of the total variation in the data. The PCA should therefore be considered alongside the sample-distance heatmap, metadata, quality-control information and statistical model.
Taken together, the statement is far too strong and over-interprets the data. There is no single correct answer but a balanced interpretation should combine the evidence without claiming that sample status caused the observed differences. It is fine to conclude that the results support an association while more evidence is needed to determine its cause.
Observations supported directly by the analyses

The MA plot shows estimated fold changes across gene abundance.
The volcano plot shows genes with different combinations of effect size and statistical evidence.
The annotated results identify some of the genes contributing to the pattern.
The PCA shows a broad distinction between the groups, particularly along PC1.
The heatmap shows that many HAT samples have relatively similar expression profiles and that distances between groups are generally larger.
Neither group is completely uniform, and the SERO TL+ samples show noticeable within-group variation.

Possible interpretations
The pattern could reflect:

biological differences associated with symptomatic and asymptomatic infection
differences in immune activity
differences in the proportions of blood-cell types
variation in infection history or other clinical characteristics
batch, sample handling or another technical variable

These are hypotheses suggested by the pattern. The plots do not distinguish between them.
Suitable follow-up investigations

colouring or shaping the PCA points by potential explanatory metadata
checking whether sample processing or batch aligns with the PCA or heatmap structure
adding relevant variables to the DESeq2 model
examining blood-cell counts or estimated cell composition
investigating whether related annotated genes participate in shared biological processes
testing whether the pattern is reproduced in an independent dataset










TipOptional Activity 2: Investigate sensitivity to the number of genes



In the main workflow, the PCA was calculated using the 500 genes with the greatest variation across the samples. This helps the PCA focus on genes that contribute most strongly to differences among samples.
However, selecting 500 genes is an analytical choice rather than a universal rule, although it is the default threshold that DESeq2 uses. In this activity, you will investigate whether the main sample pattern is sensitive to the number of variable genes included in the PCA.
This is a controlled sensitivity analysis. The aim is to determine whether the broad interpretation is stable, not a fishing exercise to select whichever number of genes produces the strongest separation.
Modify the PCA code to examine the PCA using:

the 100 most variable genes
the 1,000 most variable genes

Keep everything else unchanged so that the number of genes is the only difference between the analyses.
For each analysis, your code should:

call plotPCA() using the required ntop value
retain the same transformed object and grouping variable
create and display the PCA plot
record the percentage of variation represented by PC1 and PC2

Compare the PCA plots produced using 100, 500 and 1,000 genes.

Does the broad separation between HAT and SERO TL+ remain visible?
Do the same samples remain close together?
Does any sample move noticeably relative to the others?
Does the apparent variation within either status group change?
How does the percentage of variation explained by PC1 and PC2 change?
Which features are stable across all three analyses?
Which features appear sensitive to the number of genes selected?
Does one analysis lead to a substantially different biological interpretation?
Why would it be inappropriate to report only the plot showing the strongest separation?
Why should the 500-gene version remain the main reported analysis unless a different choice was specified in advance?

Summarise your findings by filling in the following:
The broad PCA pattern was __________ across the three analyses.

The main stable features were __________.

The features most affected by the number of genes were __________.

This suggests that our interpretation is __________ to the number of
variable genes included.








TipPossible guided solution





The broad PCA pattern is similar when the analysis is repeated using 100, 500 and 1000 variable genes.
In all three plots:

the HAT and SERO TL+ samples are separated mainly along PC1
most HAT samples have negative PC1 coordinates
most SERO TL+ samples have positive PC1 coordinates
there is noticeable variation within both groups
some samples are separated from other members of the same status group along PC2

This suggests that the main distinction between the HAT and SERO TL+ samples is reasonably robust to the number of variable genes included. The separation is therefore unlikely to depend entirely on the exact choice of 500 genes.
However, the plots are not identical. The positions of individual samples, the spread within each group and the relative importance of PC1 and PC2 can change when different genes are included. This is expected because each PCA is calculated from a different expression matrix. The analysis using 100 genes is based on a relatively small set of the most variable genes. It may therefore be influenced strongly by a few genes with particularly large variation. The analysis using 1,000 genes includes more of the expression data but some of the additional genes may contribute relatively little to the main sample differences.
This suggests that sample status is associated with a major source of expression variation in these data but they do not demonstrate that status causes the separation. Other biological or technical variables associated with status could also contribute to the pattern.
The 500-gene PCA should remain the main reported analysis because it was the choice made in the original workflow. The 100- and 1,000-gene analyses provide evidence that the broad interpretation is not highly sensitive to this choice. It would not be appropriate to select one of the alternative plots simply because it appears to show the strongest separation.

  selected_vsd,
  intgroup = "status",
  ntop = 100,
  returnData = TRUE
)

using ntop=100 top features by variance

  pca_data_100,
  aes(
    x = PC1,
    y = PC2,
    colour = group
  )
) +
  geom_point()

#build and plot the top 1000 gene pca

  selected_vsd,
  intgroup = "status",
  ntop = 1000,
  returnData = TRUE
)

using ntop=1000 top features by variance

  pca_data_1000,

    y = PC2,

  )

NoteLearning outcomes



By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

explain why titles, axis labels, legends, readable text and colour choices affect the clarity and accessibility of a figure;
identify the data, aesthetic mappings and geometry used in a ggplot2 figure;
distinguish between mapping a variable inside aes() and setting an appearance outside aes();

ISCB alignment: D3 (select and refine visual representations appropriate to different RNA-seq results), E3 (update analysis scripts and save clearly labelled figures using reproducible filenames and dimensions), H3 (use ggplot2 mappings, geometries, scales, themes and annotation layers to customise figures in R), K3 (communicate results through clear, accessible figures, legends and reproducibly selected labels).









TipRecap: If the objects are not available






library(DESeq2)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)

# Import the original data
count_data <- as.matrix(
  read.csv(
    "m_sample_counts.csv",
    row.names = 1,
    check.names = FALSE
  )
)

sample_info <- read.csv(
  "m_sample_info.csv",
  row.names = 1,
  check.names = FALSE
)

sample_info <- sample_info[
  colnames(count_data),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

sample_info$status <- factor(sample_info$status)

# Sample-level summary
sample_summary <- data.frame(
  sample_id = colnames(count_data),
  status = sample_info$status,
  total_counts = colSums(count_data),
  detected_genes = colSums(count_data > 0)
)

# Long-format count data
count_plot_data <- stack(
  as.data.frame(log2(count_data + 1))
)

colnames(count_plot_data) <- c(
  "log2_count",
  "sample_id"
)

# Load the fitted DESeq2 object
dds_fitted <- readRDS(
  "objects/dds_fitted.rds"
)

# HAT-versus-SERO result
res_hat_vs_sero <- results(
  dds_fitted,
  contrast = c("status", "hat", "sero"),
  alpha = 0.05
)

result_data <- data.frame(
  gene_id = rownames(res_hat_vs_sero),
  as.data.frame(res_hat_vs_sero),
  row.names = NULL
)

# Add gene symbols
annotation_data <- read.csv(
  "human_annotations_from_orgHs.csv",
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

symbol_column <- if (
  "SYMBOL_SAFE" %in% colnames(annotation_data)
) {
  "SYMBOL_SAFE"
} else {
  "SYMBOL"
}

result_data$symbol <- annotation_data[[symbol_column]][
  match(
    result_data$gene_id,
    annotation_data$ENSEMBL
  )
]

missing_symbol <- is.na(result_data$symbol) |
  result_data$symbol == ""

result_data$symbol[missing_symbol] <-
  result_data$gene_id[missing_symbol]

# Volcano-plot data
plot_de <- result_data[
  !is.na(result_data$padj),
]

plot_de$minus_log10_padj <-
  -log10(plot_de$padj)

plot_de$direction <- "Below thresholds"

plot_de$direction[
  plot_de$padj < 0.05 &
    plot_de$log2FoldChange > 1
] <- "Higher in HAT"

plot_de$direction[
  plot_de$padj < 0.05 &
    plot_de$log2FoldChange < -1
] <- "Higher in SERO TL+"

# VST data for the single-gene plot, PCA and distances
vsd <- vst(
  dds_fitted,
  blind = FALSE
)

selected_samples <- rownames(sample_info)[
  sample_info$status %in% c("hat", "sero")
]

selected_vsd <- vsd[
  ,
  selected_samples
]

selected_vst <- assay(selected_vsd)

# PCA data
pca_data <- plotPCA(
  selected_vsd,
  intgroup = "status",
  ntop = 500,
  returnData = TRUE
)

pc1_percent <- round(
  100 * attr(pca_data, "percentVar")[1],
  1
)

pc2_percent <- round(
  100 * attr(pca_data, "percentVar")[2],
  1
)

# Sample-distance data
sample_dist_matrix <- as.matrix(
  dist(t(selected_vst))
)

distance_data <- as.data.frame(
  as.table(sample_dist_matrix)
)

colnames(distance_data) <- c(
  "sample_1",
  "sample_2",
  "distance"
)

# Recreate the original plot objects
read_plot <- ggplot(
  sample_summary,
  aes(x = sample_id, y = total_counts)
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip()

count_distribution_plot <- ggplot(
  count_plot_data,
  aes(x = sample_id, y = log2_count)
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip()

distance_plot <- ggplot(
  distance_data,
  aes(
    x = sample_1,
    y = sample_2,
    fill = distance
  )
) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  coord_equal()

volcano_plot <- ggplot(
  plot_de,
  aes(
    x = log2FoldChange,
    y = minus_log10_padj,
    colour = direction
  )
) +
  geom_point()

pca_plot <- ggplot(
  pca_data,
  aes(
    x = PC1,
    y = PC2,
    colour = group
  )
) +
  geom_point()
