text:
9.4 Building a ggplot2 figure
We will begin by plotting the expression of IRF8, the gene with the smallest adjusted p-value in our earlier differential-expression analysis. Its Ensembl gene ID is ENSG00000140968.
First, we will use the Ensembl gene ID to select the IRF8 expression values, then combine them with the clinical group for each sample:

gene_data <- data.frame(
  expression = selected_vst["ENSG00000140968", ],
  status = sample_info[
    colnames(selected_vst),
    "status"
  ]
)

head(gene_data)

     expression status
h1.1   11.32466    hat
h1.2   11.20217    hat
h1.3   11.62455    hat
h1.5   11.54062    hat
h2.2   11.93360    hat
h2.3   11.74337    hat


This is similar to how we constructed sample_summary in Chapter 2. The new data frame contains:

expression, containing the expression of ENSG00000140968 in each sample;
status, containing the clinical group of each sample.

Each row of gene_data represents one sample.
A ggplot2 figure needs three main pieces:

a data frame;
columns to place on the axes;
a way to draw each observation.

We can plot out the VST expression of ENSG00000140968 for HAT and SERO TL+ using:

gene_plot <- ggplot(
  gene_data,
  aes(
    x = status,
    y = expression
  )
) +
  geom_point()

gene_plot








We can interpret this code as:
Use gene_data, place status on the x-axis, place expression on the y-axis, and draw each sample as a point.
In the code:

ggplot(gene_data) selects the data;
aes(x = status, y = expression) connects columns in the data to the axes;
geom_point() draws one point for each row;
<- stores the figure as gene_plot;
typing gene_plot displays it.

The instructions inside aes() are called aesthetic mappings. They connect columns in the data to visual features of the plot. Here, the status column controls horizontal position and the expression column controls vertical position.

9.4.1 Make the individual samples visible
In this simple figure, samples in the same group have the same horizontal position so some points may overlap. We can replace geom_point() with geom_jitter() to spread them slightly from side to side to avoid this:

gene_plot <- ggplot(
  gene_data,
  aes(
    x = status,
    y = expression
  )
) +
  geom_jitter(
    width = 0.08,
    size = 3,
    colour = "blue"
  )

gene_plot








The x and y positions still come from columns in gene_data. The arguments inside geom_jitter() are fixed settings that control how the points are drawn. We can change these settings to improve the readability of the plot:

width = 0.08 controls how far the points can move horizontally;
size = 3 makes every point larger;
colour = "blue" makes every point blue.



9.4.2 Add a summary layer and clear labels
A ggplot2 figure can contain several layers. We can add a boxplot to summarise each group while retaining the points for the individual samples:

gene_plot <- ggplot(
  gene_data,
  aes(
    x = status,
    y = expression
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.55,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    colour = "grey35"
  ) +
  geom_jitter(
    width = 0.08,
    size = 3,
    colour = "blue"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Expression of IRF8",
    x = "Clinical group",
    y = "Variance-stabilised expression"
  )

gene_plot








The two layers have different roles:

geom_boxplot() summarises the distribution within each group;
geom_jitter() shows the individual samples.

At this stage, colour is a fixed setting. Every point is blue. We will introduce mapping a data column to colour when we reach the PCA, where colour adds information that is not already shown on an axis.


9.4.3 Colour names and hexadecimal codes
R recognises many colour names. These are a small selection:
"red"
"blue"
"orange"
"purple"
"black"
"grey"
"darkgreen"
"steelblue"
Colour names are a clear starting point. You can also use a hexadecimal (hex) colour code when you want a precise shade:
colour = "#0072B2"
The R colour-name and hexadecimal-code reference shows the colours available in R alongside their names and hex colour codes.






ImportantChoose colours that remain distinguishable



Avoid relying on similar colours or a red-green combination to distinguish important groups. These can be difficult to distinguish for people with some forms of colour-vision deficiency or other visual impairments. Use colours with clear contrast, and have clear axis labels, plot legends or other information so that colour is not the only way to identify the groups.




9.4.4 Adding clear labels
A reader should also be able to identify what the figure shows and what each axis represents.
The labs() function adds labels to a ggplot2 figure:
labs(
  title = "Expression of IRF8",
  x = "Clinical group",
  y = "Variance-stabilised expression"
)
Here:

title describes what the figure shows;
x provides a clear label for the x-axis;
y identifies the measurement shown on the y-axis.

These labels replace the original column names, status and expression, with wording that is more meaningful to a reader.
Good labels should:

describe the data rather than expose the R column names;
state any transformation or normalisation where relevant;
include measurement units where appropriate;
remain short enough to read easily.

For example, "Variance-stabilised expression" is more informative than "expression" because it tells the reader that the expression values have been transformed.






NoteTitles, plot legends and figure legends



These parts of a figure have different purposes:

the title states what the figure is about
the axis labels explain the variables or measurements
the plot legend, or key, explains colours, shapes or other visual features
the figure legend, or caption, provides the information needed to interpret the complete figure

They should work together rather than repeat exactly the same information.

9.5 Compare built-in themes
We can also improve our figures by using a theme. A theme changes the background, grid lines, axes and text used by a ggplot2 figure all at the same time. It does not change the data or the variables shown.
Compare three built-in themes:

gene_plot + theme_bw()









gene_plot + theme_classic()









gene_plot + theme_minimal()








When we look at the different figures:

Which version makes the data easiest to see?
Are the grid lines helpful or distracting?
Are the axes and labels clear?
Which theme has the least unnecessary visual clutter?

There is no single best theme for every figure. Choose one that keeps the data clear and suits the purpose of the plot.
You can also use the base_size argument inside a theme function to control the general text size used by the theme.
For the worked examples in this chapter, we will use theme_classic(base_size = 12) as this is generally readable by most people.

gene_plot <- gene_plot +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)

gene_plot

text:
9.6 Figure legends
A figure legend, sometimes called a figure caption, is the short description placed underneath a figure. It should allow a reader to understand the figure without needing to inspect the R code.
A useful figure legend should briefly explain:

what is being shown
what each point, bar, box or tile represents
the groups or comparison being made
any transformation or important threshold
the main visual encodings, such as colour or shape

A figure legend is different from the plot legend, or key, that appears inside or beside a plot. The plot legend explains visual features such as colours and shapes. The figure legend explains the figure as a whole. Typically, legends have a short title that precedes the legend itself.
For example, for the single-gene expression plot we could write:
Expression of IRF8 in HAT and SERO TL+ samples. Each point represents the variance-stabilised expression value for one sample. Boxes summarise the distribution within each clinical group.
We will practice writing legends to describe our figures as we work through the session.

9.7 Improve the total-count bar chart
Return to the read_plot code in your original script. The default column names sample_id and total_counts are useful in code, but they are not polished figure labels.

read_plot <- ggplot(
  sample_summary,
  aes(x = sample_id, y = total_counts)
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip()
  
read_plot








First, we can add a title and axis labels:

read_plot <- ggplot(
  sample_summary,
  aes(x = sample_id, y = total_counts)
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Total RNA-seq counts for each sample",
    x = "Sample",
    y = "Total counts"
  )

read_plot








The title states the purpose of the plot. The axis labels use readable language rather than object names.
Next, we can map status to the bar fill and specify the colours directly in the plot code:

read_plot <- ggplot(
  sample_summary,
  aes(
    x = sample_id,
    y = total_counts,
    fill = status
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      ctrl = "grey",
      sero = "blue",
      hat = "orange"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Total RNA-seq counts for each sample",
    x = "Sample",
    y = "Total counts",
    fill = "Clinical group"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)

read_plot








Here, fill = status is inside aes() because bar fill represents a column in the data. scale_fill_manual() specifies the colour used for each group.






NoteWhat does c() mean here?



The c() function combines values into a vector:
c(
  ctrl = "grey",
  sero = "blue",
  hat = "orange"
)
We provide three colours because status has three groups in sample_summary. Each group is matched to one colour. Naming the colours makes the intended mapping explicit rather than relying on the order of the factor levels. If there were two groups we would supply two colours, if there were four we would supply four etc.


Find the original read_plot section in your script and replace it with the improved version. Then save the updated plot using the same filename as before.






TipSolution






ggsave(
  filename = "figures/total_counts_per_sample.png",
  plot = read_plot
)

what the bar length shows
what the fill colours identify

Total RNA-seq counts for each sample. Each bar represents one sample and bar length shows the total number of counts assigned to that sample. The bar fill colour identifies the clinical group.

9.8 Improve the count-distribution boxplot
Earlier, we created the count-distribution boxplot to compare the distribution of gene counts across samples. Each box summarised the log-transformed counts for all genes in one sample.
The original plot was useful for exploring the data but its labels and appearance can be improved to make it easier for another reader to interpret.
For example, the count-distribution plot should explain what has been transformed. An axis label such as log2_count is ambiguous to a reader and we should state the calculation explicitly as log2(count + 1).
We also want to colour the boxes by clinical group. However, count_plot_data currently contains only the count value and sample ID:

head(count_plot_data)

  log2_count sample_id
1   3.584963      h1.1
2   0.000000      h1.1
3   7.918863      h1.1
4   9.033423      h1.1
5   6.375039      h1.1
6  13.776844      h1.1


The clinical group is stored separately in sample_info. Before we can use fill = status in the plot, we need to add the correct status to every row of count_plot_data. We can do this with match() as we did before:

count_plot_data$status <- sample_info$status[
  match(
    count_plot_data$sample_id,
    rownames(sample_info)
  )
]

The match() function connects the two data frames using their sample IDs:

count_plot_data$sample_id contains the sample ID for each count;
rownames(sample_info) contains the sample IDs in the sample information;
sample_info$status contains the clinical group we want to retrieve.

The result is a new column called status:

head(count_plot_data)

  log2_count sample_id status
1   3.584963      h1.1    hat
2   0.000000      h1.1    hat
3   7.918863      h1.1    hat
4   9.033423      h1.1    hat
5   6.375039      h1.1    hat
6  13.776844      h1.1    hat


Each row now contains:

the log-transformed count;
the sample ID;
the clinical group.

This means that we can now map status to box fill:
aes(
  x = sample_id,
  y = log2_count,
  fill = status
)

give the plot legend a readable title;

Which code belongs inside aes() and which code fixes the appearance of the plot?

count_distribution_plot <- ggplot(
  count_plot_data,
  aes(
    x = sample_id,
    y = log2_count,
    fill = status
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      ctrl = "grey",
      sero = "blue",
      hat = "orange"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of gene counts in each sample",
    x = "Sample",
    y = "log2(count + 1)",
    fill = "Clinical group"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)

count_distribution_plot








fill = status belongs inside aes() because fill represents a column in the data.

ggsave(
  filename = "/count_distributions_per_sample.png",
  plot = count_distribution_plot
)

9.9 Improve the sample-distance heatmap
The sample-distance heatmap already uses scale_fill_viridis_c(). A heatmap uses fill to represent a continuous numerical value, so its plot legend is the equivalent of an axis and should have a meaningful title.

distance_plot <- ggplot(

text:
9.10 Improve the PCA plot
The PCA is useful for explaining how to map a data column to colour because the clinical group is not already shown on an axis.

pca_plot <- ggplot(
  pca_data,
  aes(
    x = PC1,
    y = PC2,
    colour = group,
    shape = group
  )
) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      sero = "blue",
      hat = "orange"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "PCA of HAT and SERO TL+ expression profiles",
    x = paste0("PC1 (", pc1_percent, "%)"),
    y = paste0("PC2 (", pc2_percent, "%)"),
    colour = "Clinical group",
    shape = "Clinical group"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)

pca_plot








The plot uses four aesthetic mappings:

x = PC1 maps PC1 to horizontal position
y = PC2 maps PC2 to vertical position
colour = group maps clinical group to point colour
shape = group maps clinical group to point shape

Because colour = group is inside aes(), colour represents a column in the data and ggplot2 creates a plot legend. scale_colour_manual() then specifies which colour represents each group.
By contrast, size = 4 is outside aes() because it is a fixed setting applied to every point.
Because colour and shape are mapped to group, they vary between clinical groups and appear in the plot legend.
Because size is set to 4, every sample has the same point size and no separate size legend is created.
Save the Revised PCA Plot
Make sure to save the revised PCA plot:

ggsave(
  filename = "figures/PCA_sero_hat.png",
  plot = pca_plot
)

TipPossible answer





Principal component analysis of HAT and SERO TL+ expression profiles. Each point represents one sample positioned according to its variance-stabilised gene-expression profile. The axis labels show the percentage of variation explained by PC1 and PC2. Point colour and shape identify the clinical group.

9.11 Improve the volcano plot
The volcano plot contains thousands of genes, so clarity depends on restraint. Larger points can help, but points that are too large will hide the density of the data:

volcano_plot <- ggplot(
  plot_de,
  aes(
    x = log2FoldChange,
    y = minus_log10_padj,
    colour = direction
  )
) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = c(-1, 1),
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = -log10(0.05),
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Below thresholds" = "grey",
      "Higher in HAT" = "orange",
      "Higher in SERO TL+" = "blue"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Differential expression: HAT versus SERO TL+",
    x = "Log2 fold change (HAT versus SERO TL+)",
    y = "-log10 adjusted p-value",
    colour = "Result category"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)

volcano_plot









9.11.1 Labelling points
The volcano plot shows thousands of genes, but it does not currently identify individual genes.
We could add a label to every point, but the labels would overlap and make the figure difficult to read. Instead, we will label a small number of genes selected using a clear rule.
Here, we will label the five genes with the smallest adjusted p-values among those that pass both thresholds.

9.11.1.1 Select genes that pass both thresholds
When we constructed the data for the volcano plot, the direction column identified genes that are:

"Higher in HAT";
"Higher in SERO TL+";
"Below thresholds".

For labelling the volcano plot, we filter down to the genes with the lowest adjusted p value. First, we use subsetting and indexing to keep only genes that are not in the "Below thresholds" category:

label_candidates <- plot_de[
  plot_de$direction != "Below thresholds",
]

Some genes may not have an available gene symbol so we’ll remove these before creating the labels:

label_candidates <- label_candidates[
  !is.na(label_candidates$symbol) &
    label_candidates$symbol != "",
]

9.11.1.2 Select five genes
Sort the candidate genes by adjusted p-value:

label_candidates <- label_candidates[
  order(label_candidates$padj),
]

The genes with the smallest adjusted p-values are now at the top of the data frame.

#Keep the first five rows of label_candidates
label_genes <- head(label_candidates,5)

The five genes are selected using a reproducible rule rather than chosen because they look interesting on the finished plot.
Another valid rule might be to label genes with the largest absolute fold changes. Whichever rule is used should be stated in the figure legend.


9.11.1.3 Add labels with ggrepel
The ggrepel package provides the geom_label_repel() function. It works like geom_label() but attempts to move labels away from one another and from the points they identify (ggplot text labels repel each other).
To make the labels clearer on the plot:

colour = "black" fixes the label text colourto black
fill = "white" gives every label a white background so that it remains readable over the coloured points


volcano_plot <- volcano_plot +
  geom_label_repel(
    data = label_genes,
    aes(label = symbol),
    colour = "black",
    fill = "white",
    size = 3.5,
    show.legend = FALSE
  )

volcano_plot








This new layer uses:
data = label_genes
This means that labels are added only for the five rows in label_genes. The points in the original volcano plot are unaffected.
The following mapping tells ggplot2 what text to display:
aes(label = symbol)
Each selected point is labelled using the value in its symbol column.
The x- and y-axis mappings do not need to be repeated. The label layer inherits these from the original volcano_plot:
x = log2FoldChange
y = minus_log10_padj
Therefore, each label is placed near the point representing the same gene.
The remaining arguments control the appearance of the labels:

size = 3.5 controls the text size;
show.legend = FALSE prevents the text layer from adding another entry to the plot legend.

Unlike geom_text() or geom_label(), geom_label_repel() attempts to move labels apart and adds small connecting lines where needed. This makes a small number of labels easier to read.






ImportantLabels should improve the figure



Adding more labels does not always add more information. Too many labels can cover the points and make the overall pattern difficult to see.
Use a small number of labels, state how they were selected and check that they remain readable at the final figure size.


Make sure to save your revised figure:

ggsave(
  filename = "figures/volcano_hat_vs_sero_labelled.png",
  plot = volcano_plot
)

Differential expression between HAT and SERO TL+ samples. Each point represents one gene. Positive log2 fold changes indicate higher estimated expression in HAT, while negative values indicate higher estimated expression in SERO TL+. Colours identify genes above and below the adjusted p-value and absolute log2 fold-change thresholds. Dashed lines show an adjusted p-value of 0.05 and log2 fold changes of -1 and 1. The five labelled genes have the smallest adjusted p-values among genes passing both thresholds.

text:
9.12 Saving figures with specific dimensions
Until now, we have allowed ggsave() to choose the dimensions of the saved figure:

ggsave(
  filename = "figures/pca_plot.png",
  plot = pca_plot
)

We can make the output more predictable by specifying its width and height. The examples below use inches as it is the default for ggplot but you can use centimetres by setting units = “cm” and supplying centimetre dimensions. These values also determine the figure’s aspect ratio, which is its shape.
Compare aspect ratios
Save the PCA plot three times using different dimensions:

ggsave(
  filename = "figures/pca_wide.png",
  plot = pca_plot,
  width = 10,
  height = 5,
  units = "in"
)

ggsave(
  filename = "figures/pca_tall.png",
  plot = pca_plot,
  width = 5,
  height = 10,
  units = "in"
)

ggsave(
  filename = "figures/pca_square.png",
  plot = pca_plot,
  width = 6,
  height = 6,
  units = "in"
)

Open the figures folder in Windows File Explorer or macOS Finder, then compare the three files.

Which dimensions make the PCA pattern easiest to interpret?
What happens to the apparent distance between points?
Which version gives enough space to the axes, title and plot legend?
Does any version make the plot feel compressed or stretched?







WarningDimensions affect interpretation



The data have not changed, but the shape of the plotting area has. An unsuitable aspect ratio can make distances and patterns appear compressed or stretched. For a PCA plot, similar width and height are usually a sensible starting point because distances in both directions are important.








TipTry it yourself: Choose dimensions for your figures



Return to the ggsave() code for each of your figures and add width, height and units.
Choose dimensions that make the figure’s main message clear and keep the title, axes, labels and plot legend easy to read.
ggsave(
  filename = "figures/your_figure.png",
  plot = your_plot,
  width = ...,
  height = ...,
  units = "in"
)
Open each file in Windows File Explorer or macOS Finder. Adjust the width and height if the figure looks crowded, compressed or unnecessarily spread out. There is no single correct size for every figure.

9.14 Optional extra activities
You have now completed the required activities for this chapter. The remaining section is an optional, but valuable challenge for further practice. You can attempt it now or return to it later.






TipOptional Activity 1: label samples on the PCA plot



The points in the PCA plot represent individual samples. Colour and shape help us identify the clinical groups, but they do not tell us which sample is represented by each point.
Adding sample labels can help us:

identify a sample that is separated from the others;
investigate possible outliers;
connect unusual PCA positions to the earlier quality-control plots;
check whether technical or biological information might explain the pattern.

Labels may not be useful in a final figure because they can make the plot crowded. However, they can be valuable while exploring and checking the data.

9.14.2 Add the sample labels
The ggrepel package provides geom_label_repel(). We used this function to add gene labels to the volcano plot. We can use the same approach to label samples on the PCA.

pca_plot_labelled <- pca_plot +
  geom_label_repel(
    aes(label = name),
    colour = "black",
    fill = "white",
    size = 3,
    show.legend = FALSE
  )

pca_plot_labelled








The following mapping tells ggplot2 which text to display:
aes(label = name)
Each point is labelled using the sample ID in the name column.
Unlike the volcano plot, we do not need to provide a separate data frame using data =. We want to label every sample, so geom_label_repel() uses all the rows in pca_data.
The remaining arguments control the appearance of the labels:

colour = "black" makes the label text black;
fill = "white" gives each label a white background;
size = 3 controls the text size;
show.legend = FALSE prevents the label layer from adding another entry to the plot legend.

geom_label_repel() attempts to move overlapping labels apart. It may also draw small connecting lines between labels and their points.






NoteUse the labelled plot to investigate samples



Look for samples that:

are positioned far from other samples in the same group;
are positioned between the clinical groups;
appear unusual in both the PCA and earlier quality-control figures.

An unusual PCA position does not automatically mean that a sample should be removed. It identifies a sample that may be worth investigating further.
Return to the total-count and count-distribution plots and check whether the same sample also has an unusual library size or count distribution.




9.14.3 Completed code
The complete labelled PCA can be created with:

pca_plot_labelled <- ggplot(
  pca_data,
  aes(
    x = PC1,
    y = PC2,
    colour = group,
    shape = group
  )
) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_label_repel(
    aes(label = name),
    colour = "black",
    fill = "white",
    size = 3,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      sero = "blue",
      hat = "orange"
    )
  ) +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c(
      sero = 16,
      hat = 17
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "PCA of HAT and SERO TL+ expression profiles",
    x = paste0("PC1 (", pc1_percent, "%)"),
    y = paste0("PC2 (", pc2_percent, "%)"),
    colour = "Clinical group",
    shape = "Clinical group"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)

pca_plot_labelled














ImportantDecide whether the labels help



The labelled PCA is useful for exploring the data, but it may not be the clearest version for a report or presentation.
Compare pca_plot and pca_plot_labelled. Use the labelled version to identify samples during quality control but use the unlabelled version if the labels obscure the overall PCA pattern.


If you want to save the labelled version separately:

ggsave(
  filename = "figures/PCA_sero_hat_labelled.png",
  plot = pca_plot_labelled
)










TipOptional Activity 2: Create your own theme



Built-in themes provide a quick way to change the overall appearance of a plot. You can also create your own theme to control specific features, such as the size, colour and alignment of text.
In this worked example, we will customise the total-count plot but the theme you build can be applied to all your figures.
Start with a built-in theme
First, apply a built-in theme to control the general appearance:

read_plot +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)








We can then use theme() to modify individual parts of the plot.

read_plot +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      size = 16,
      face = "bold"
    ),
    axis.title = element_text(
      size = 12,
      face = "bold"
    ),
    axis.text = element_text(
      size = 10
    ),
    legend.title = element_text(
      size = 11,
      face = "bold"
    )
  )








The theme() function controls the supporting elements of a plot, such as:

the title;
axis titles;
axis labels;
legend text;
grid lines;
the plot background.

It does not change the data, mappings or geometries.
Inside theme(), we identify the part of the plot that we want to change:
plot.title
axis.title
axis.text
legend.title
element_text() describes how a text element should appear. Some useful arguments are:
element_text(
  size = 14,
  face = "bold",
  colour = "navy",
  hjust = 0.5
)
Here:

size controls the text size;
face can be "plain", "bold" or "italic";
colour changes the text colour;
hjust controls horizontal alignment.

For a plot title, hjust = 0 places the title on the left, while hjust = 0.5 centres it.
Storing a custom theme
If the same formatting will be used on several plots, it can be stored as an object:

my_theme <- theme(
  plot.title = element_text(
    size = 16,
    face = "bold",
    hjust = 0.5
  ),
  axis.title = element_text(
    size = 12,
    face = "bold"
  ),
  axis.text = element_text(
    size = 10
  ),
  legend.title = element_text(
    size = 11,
    face = "bold"
  )
)

The object my_theme contains only the additional formatting choices. It does not contain any data or create a plot by itself.
Apply the built-in theme first, followed by the custom changes:

read_plot <- read_plot +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  my_theme

read_plot








The order matters. If two themes change the same feature, the theme added last takes priority.








TipTry it yourself: Customise another plot



Apply theme_classic() and my_theme to pca_plot. Then modify at least one setting in my_theme. Save the result as pca_plot_custom.








TipPossible Solution





This example left-aligns the title and changes its colour:

pca_theme <- theme(
  plot.title = element_text(
    size = 16,
    face = "bold",
    colour = "navy",
    hjust = 0
  ),
  axis.title = element_text(
    size = 12,
    face = "bold"
  ),
  axis.text = element_text(
    size = 10
  ),
  legend.title = element_text(
    size = 11,
    face = "bold"
  )
)

pca_plot_custom <- pca_plot +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  pca_theme

pca_plot_custom








Your choices do not need to match this example. Check that the finished title, axes and legend remain clear and that the formatting does not distract from the PCA pattern.









TipOptional Activity 3: combine plots into a multi-panel figure



Individual plots are often combined into a multi-panel figure for a report, presentation or publication. Each panel may show a different type of data, but the plots should contribute to one overall message.
In this worked example, we will combine the total-count bar chart and count-distribution boxplot into a single sample quality-control figure.
Panels combine separate plot objects, which may use different data or different geometries.
Here, read_plot and count_distribution_plot are separate plot objects, so we will combine them as panels.
Install and load patchwork
We will use the patchwork package to arrange the plots. Install it once using install.packages("patchwork") if it is not already installed:

library(patchwork)

qc_panel <- (
  read_plot + count_distribution_plot
) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "RNA-seq sample quality-control summaries",
    tag_levels = "A"
  ) &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Combine two related plots
The + operator places the two plot objects next to each other:

qc_panel <- read_plot + count_distribution_plot

qc_panel








This works, but a finished multi-panel figure should also explain how the panels are related. We can add an overall title and automatic panel labels using plot_annotation():

qc_panel <- (
  read_plot + count_distribution_plot
) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "RNA-seq sample quality-control summaries",
    tag_levels = "A"
  )

qc_panel








tag_levels = "A" adds the panel labels A and B automatically.
Collect repeated legends
Both plots use colour to represent the same clinical groups. Instead of showing the same legend twice, plot_layout() can collect the legends into one location:

qc_panel <- (
  read_plot + count_distribution_plot
) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "RNA-seq sample quality-control summaries",
    tag_levels = "A"
  ) &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

qc_panel








The & applies the theme modification to every plot in the patchwork.
Think about readability
Combining plots reduces the space available to each one. Before saving a combined figure, check:

Are the sample names still readable?
Are the axis labels large enough?
Are the panel labels easy to find?
Do colours have the same meaning in every panel?
Does the shared legend describe both plots correctly?
Would stacking the plots vertically provide more space?

If the sample labels are crowded, a vertical layout may be clearer:

qc_panel_vertical <- (
  read_plot / count_distribution_plot
) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "RNA-seq sample quality-control summaries",
    tag_levels = "A"
  ) &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

qc_panel_vertical








Which figure displays the information the best?
Save the combined figure

ggsave(
  filename = "figures/sample_qc_panel.png",
  plot = qc_panel,
  width = 12,
  height = 6,
  dpi = 300
)

A multi-panel figure should tell one coherent story. Only combine plots when their relationship is useful to the reader.

text:
10.2 Why reproducibility matters
Imagine that you complete your assessment today and revisit it several months later. Would you be able to run the analysis again and obtain the same results?
A reproducible analysis allows another person, or your future self, to:

identify the original data used
understand each analysis step
follow the reasoning behind important decisions
run the code successfully
generate the same outputs

In bioinformatics, reproducibility is especially important because analyses often involve multiple files, software packages, parameters, and processing steps.
Good reproducibility habits include:

keeping project files organised
writing clear code that runs in a logical order
adding useful comments
recording important analysis decisions and settings
recording software and package versions
sharing code and data responsibly







TipA useful question



For each result in your assessment, ask:

Could another student understand how I produced this result without me explaining it to them?
crumbs: 10  Assessment Workshop and R Catch-up

title: 10  Assessment Workshop and R Catch-up
text:
10.3 Commenting and documenting code
You may have noticed that some lines in R code begin with a hash symbol, #. These lines are called comments.
R ignores everything after # on that line. Comments are written for people reading the code and are not treated as instructions for R.
Comments can help us:

explain the purpose of a section of code
record why an analytic decision was made
make a script easier to navigate
help someone else understand and reuse our analysis
remind our future selves what the code was intended to do

A useful comment normally explains why a function is being run or what a group of statements is intended to achieve. It should not simply repeat something that is already obvious from the code.
For example, this comment is not especially helpful:
# Use dim on count_data
dim(count_data)
This version better explains the purpose of the statement at this point in the script:
# Confirm the number of imported genes (rows) and samples (columns)
dim(count_data)
Comments can also record an important analysis decision:
# Remove genes with fewer than 10 counts across all samples
# to reduce noise from very low-count genes.
count_data <- count_data[rowSums(count_data) >= 10, ]
The comment explains the purpose of the filtering step and records the threshold that was used.
Comments should be useful but concise. Too many comments can make a script harder to read, particularly when every simple function has a comment that merely repeats the code.






TipQuick check



Which comment would be more useful to someone reviewing your project several months later?
# Make volcano plot
ggplot(...)
or
# Visualise differential expression results and highlight genes
# meeting the significance threshold used in the report.
ggplot(...)
The second comment is more useful because it describes the purpose of the figure rather than simply naming the type of plot.



10.3.1 Use headings to organise a script
Comments can also divide a longer script into sections. RStudio recognises section headings written in this form:
# Import data -------------------------------------------------------------

# Check sample identifiers ------------------------------------------------

# Filter low-count genes --------------------------------------------------

# Differential expression analysis ---------------------------------------

# Create figures ----------------------------------------------------------

# Save outputs ------------------------------------------------------------
This makes the script easier to scan and provides navigation in RStudio’s document outline.


10.3.2 Record decisions, not just commands
Some information cannot be reconstructed from the code alone. Record decisions such as:

why a filtering threshold was chosen
why a sample was excluded
which group was used as the reference level
which statistical test or model was selected
whether default settings were changed
where the original data came from

These details may be recorded in comments, the assessment report, or a short README.md file.
A useful README.md might state:

the purpose of the project
where the data came from
the order in which scripts should be run
which outputs the scripts create
any important assumptions or decisions







ImportantMini audit: improve one comment



Find one comment in your assessment code that only repeats the command below it. Rewrite the comment so that it explains the purpose of the step or the reason for the decision.
If the code is already self-explanatory and no explanation is needed, consider removing the comment instead.

10.4 Recording your session information
Good scientific practice means recording which software versions produced your results. R and its packages are updated over time, and changes between versions can affect how code behaves.
The following code saves the details of your current R session in the project rather than only printing them to the Console:

# Create the output folders if they do not already exist.
dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(
  file.path("results", "tables"),
  recursive = TRUE,
  showWarnings = FALSE
)

# Record the R, operating-system, and loaded-package versions used.
writeLines("tables/sessionInfo.txt")

tables/sessionInfo.txt


Open tables/sessionInfo.txt and inspect its contents. It records your R version, operating system, and the version of every package loaded in the current session.






NoteWhat else should be recorded?



Software versions are only one part of reproducibility. You should also be able to identify:

inputs: the files or objects used
parameters: thresholds, factor levels, and non-default settings
processing: the steps applied and their order
outputs: the files, tables, and figures produced
decisions: exclusions, transformations, and analytical choices









ImportantReproducibility check



Restart R in RStudio using Session > Restart R, and then run your script from the beginning, in order, with no earlier objects left in the Environment pane.
A reproducible workflow must not silently depend on objects created in an earlier session. If something fails, that is useful information. It means a later step depends on something that has not been created or loaded by the script.

text:
10.5 Sharing projects responsibly with GitHub
Git is a version-control system that records changes to files. GitHub is an online service that can store Git repositories and support sharing and collaboration.
For this session, the aim is not to learn every Git feature. The focus is on three practical ideas:

keeping a history of changes to analysis code
sharing code and documentation
preventing sensitive data from being added to a repository

A bioinformatics repository might contain:

R scripts
Quarto or R Markdown files
a README.md file
small, non-sensitive example data where sharing is permitted
figures or tables, where appropriate

A public repository should not contain:

identifiable or confidential patient data
files that you do not have permission to share
passwords, access tokens, or other credentials
assessment material that should not be made public







WarningData protection and research ethics



The sample data used in this activity are derived from patients. Do not upload the sample data to GitHub.
Whether research data can be shared depends on matters such as consent, identifiability, ethical approval, data-sharing agreements, and University policy. A file being technically easy to upload does not mean that uploading it is permitted.
Consult the University of Glasgow guidance when working with research data:

Data protection and freedom of information guidance for staff and students
Research ethics policy and guidance




10.5.1 Use .gitignore to exclude files
A .gitignore file tells Git which files and folders it should not track. You will be provided with a .gitignore file for the course project.
It will include rules similar to these:
# Do not track the folder containing patient-derived sample data.
data/

# Do not track common R workspace files.
.Rhistory
.RData

# Do not track operating-system files.
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db
The data/ rule prevents files inside that folder from being added to Git. The other rules exclude local files that are not needed to reproduce the analysis.






ImportantImportant limitation



A .gitignore file helps prevent files from being added accidentally, but it is not a security system.
If sensitive data have already been committed, adding the file to .gitignore does not remove the data from the repository’s earlier history. Check what will be committed before publishing or sharing a repository.








TipDiscussion: what should be shared?



For each item below, discuss whether it would normally be appropriate to upload it to a public GitHub repository:

analysis scripts
Quarto files
a README file
processed summary figures
raw patient data
metadata containing personal identifiers
a password or access token used by a script

What additional information would you need before deciding? There may not be one answer that applies to every project.




10.5.2 Install GitHub Desktop
GitHub Desktop provides a graphical interface for Git and is available for Windows and macOS.

Download and install GitHub Desktop.
Open it and sign in with your GitHub account, or create an account if required.
Clone the course repository using the URL provided by your instructor.
Choose a suitable location for the repository on your computer.
Open the repository folder and identify the analysis files, data/ folder, and results/ folder.
In GitHub Desktop, inspect the repository and confirm that the patient-derived files inside data/ are not listed as changes to be committed.







NoteGit, GitHub, and GitHub Desktop




Git tracks changes to files on your computer.
GitHub can store and share a copy of a Git repository online.
GitHub Desktop provides buttons and menus for common Git operations.

You can use Git without GitHub, and you can interact with GitHub without using the command line.




10.5.3 Make one small, meaningful commit
Make a small improvement to a comment or to the project README. In GitHub Desktop:

inspect the changed file before committing it
confirm that no data files are included
write a short commit summary describing the change, for example, Clarify count filtering decision
commit the change to the repository

A commit records a meaningful point in the history of the project. Short, specific commit messages are more useful than messages such as changes or update.

text:
10.6 R catch-up: quick review
Before moving on to more advanced topics, let’s make sure some R fundamentals from earlier chapters have properly stuck.






TipTry it yourself: quick review



Without looking back at earlier chapters, answer these from memory, then check your answers against your own earlier code:

What is the difference between count_data[1, ] and count_data[, 1]?
Why do we convert sample_info$status to a factor before analysis and plotting?
What does match(x, table) return?
In a ggplot2 call, what is the difference between putting colour = status inside aes() and writing colour = "blue" outside aes()?
Why do we always check that metadata and count-matrix samples are aligned before running a statistical test?







TipSolution






count_data[1, ] extracts the first row: one gene and all samples. count_data[, 1] extracts the first column: one sample and all genes.
Converting status to a factor with an explicit level order controls the ordering of groups in tables, legends, plots, and statistical models. It can also define the reference group used by a model.
match(x, table) returns, for each element of x, the position of its first match in table, or NA if no match is found.
Inside aes(), colour = status maps the status column to colour and creates a legend. Outside aes(), colour = "blue" applies one fixed colour to every point and does not create a mapping.
DESeq2, PCA, clustering, and plots assume that row i of the metadata and column i of the count matrix describe the same sample. A mismatch could produce technically valid output that describes the wrong biology.

10.7 Common errors and how to read them






TipTroubleshooting



object 'x' not found
You tried to use an object before creating it, or you ran chunks out of order. Rerun the script from the top and locate where the object should first be created.
non-numeric argument to binary operator
You tried to perform arithmetic on something that is not numeric. Inspect the object with class(), str(), or glimpse() before changing it.
replacement has X rows, data has Y
You tried to insert a vector of the wrong length into a data-frame column. Check that the right-hand side contains one value per row.
A plot is blank or contains no points
Check that the columns mapped inside aes() exist and contain the expected values. Inspect the data supplied to ggplot() using head(), str(), or summary().
DESeq2 reports a problem with the design formula
Check that the variable named in design = ~ status exists in colData(dds), is encoded appropriately, and contains the groups and replication expected for the analysis.








NoteA structured troubleshooting habit



When an error occurs:

read the complete error message
identify the line or chunk that failed
inspect the objects used on that line
check their names, classes, dimensions, and contents
make one change at a time, then rerun the relevant code

Do not repeatedly rerun the same command without investigating what the message is telling you.

title: 11  Pattern discovery, hierarchical clustering and heatmaps
text:
11.1 What you’ll learn
In Chapter 8, we compared the overall expression profiles of samples. In the PCA, similar samples appeared near one another. In the sample-distance heatmap, similar samples had smaller pairwise distances.
In this chapter, we will use the same idea of similarity to arrange samples into groups. This process is called clustering.
Clustering does not begin with the HAT and SERO TL+ labels. Instead, it groups objects according to patterns in the expression data. We can then compare the resulting groups with the known sample information. Because group labels are not used to construct the clustering, this is called unsupervised clustering.
Hierarchical clustering displays relationships as a branching diagram called a dendrogram. Samples or genes that join at relatively low branch heights are more similar under the selected distance and linkage rules. Objects or groups that join higher in the tree are less similar.
A clustered heatmap combines three types of information:
crumbs: 11  Pattern discovery, hierarchical clustering and heatmaps

title: 11  Pattern discovery, hierarchical clustering and heatmaps
text:
the coloured cells show expression values;
the column order shows relationships among samples;
the row order shows relationships among genes.







Important



Remember, clustering can reveal structure that is consistent with status but it cannot show that disease status caused that structure.








NoteLearning outcomes



By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

distinguish between selecting genes using statistical evidence and ordering samples and genes using hierarchical clustering
explain why gene-expression values are standardised within each gene for a pattern-focused heatmap
use a sample dendrogram to determine heatmap column order
construct and interpret a heatmap in which samples and genes are ordered using hierarchical clustering
explain how gene selection, scaling, distance and linkage affect the resulting visualisation
prepare a reproducible matrix for gene clustering in the next chapter

ISCB alignment: A3 (interpret clustering and expression patterns in their biological and experimental context), C3 (use unsupervised pattern discovery to generate cautious biological hypotheses), D3 (apply and compare Euclidean distance, hierarchical clustering, dendrograms and standardised heatmaps for high-dimensional RNA-seq data), E3 (validate intermediate objects and save documented figures, tables and reusable analysis objects), F3 (use appropriate clustering and visualisation tools for exploratory bioinformatics analysis), H3 (select, transform, reshape, order and visualise expression data in R), K3 (communicate clustering patterns and their limitations without treating visual groups as independent or causal evidence).

text:
11.2 Retrieve the previous analysis objects
We will continue to use the objects created in earlier chapters that should already be available in your R environment.






TipRecap: If the objects are not available






library(DESeq2)
library(ggplot2)

# Load the fitted model created previously
dds_fitted <- readRDS("results/objects/dds_fitted.rds")

# Retrieve aligned sample information
sample_info <- as.data.frame(colData(dds_fitted))

# Recreate the HAT-versus-SERO TL+ result
res_hat_vs_sero <- results(
  dds_fitted,
  contrast = c("status", "hat", "sero"),
  alpha = 0.05
)

# Create a results data frame with stable gene identifiers
result_data <- data.frame(
  gene_id = rownames(res_hat_vs_sero),
  as.data.frame(res_hat_vs_sero),
  row.names = NULL
)

# Sort result_data
result_data <- result_data[
  order(result_data$padj, na.last = TRUE),
]

# Add readable gene symbols
annotation_data <- read.csv(
  "human_annotations_from_orgHs.csv",
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

symbol_column <- if ("SYMBOL_SAFE" %in% colnames(annotation_data)) {
  "SYMBOL_SAFE"
} else {
  "SYMBOL"
}

result_data$symbol <- annotation_data[[symbol_column]][
  match(result_data$gene_id, annotation_data$ENSEMBL)
]

missing_symbol <- is.na(result_data$symbol) | result_data$symbol == ""
result_data$symbol[missing_symbol] <- result_data$gene_id[missing_symbol]

# Transform counts for exploratory visualisation
vsd <- vst(dds_fitted, blind = FALSE)
vst_values <- assay(vsd)

# Retain the two groups used in this comparison
selected_samples <- rownames(sample_info)[
  sample_info$status %in% c("hat", "sero")
]

selected_vst <- vst_values[
  ,
  selected_samples
]

selected_vsd <- vsd[
  ,
  selected_samples
]

selected_info <- sample_info[
  selected_samples,
]

selected_info$status <- droplevels(selected_info$status)

title: 11  Pattern discovery, hierarchical clustering and heatmaps
text:
11.3 Hierarchical clustering
In Chapter 8, each point in the PCA represented a sample and the sample-distance heatmap represented every pairwise sample comparison. Hierarchical clustering uses the same general distance information but presents it as a branching tree.






TipTry it yourself: Clustering without R



This can be difficult to follow at first, so let’s practise with a small example data frame and your own intuition:
         sample_1 sample_2 sample_3 sample_4
gene_A       2        3        8        9
gene_B       3        3        9        8

Which two samples look most similar?
Which other two samples look similar?
If you divided the samples into two groups, what would they be?
How could you represent the sequence in which the samples were grouped?









NoteSolution






sample_1 and sample_2 look the most similar. Gene A differs by 1 and Gene B has the same value in both samples.
sample_3 and sample_4 also look similar. Both samples have relatively high values for Gene A and Gene B.
A possible grouping might involve two groups where:

Group 1: contains sample_1 and sample_2
Group 2: contains sample_3 and sample_4

The sequence can be represented using a tree or dendrogram:

          ┌─ sample_1
      ┌───┤
      │   └─ sample_2
──────┤
      │   ┌─ sample_3
      └───┤
          └─ sample_4
Samples that join at a lower height are more similar according to the measurements used for clustering. The two larger groups join at a higher height because their profiles are less similar.
The groups were identified from the expression values. We did not use predefined sample labels to construct them.



In real RNA-seq data, each sample is described by expression measurements for thousands of genes. We therefore use a summary distance measure to summarise the difference between every pair of sample profiles.






TipTry it yourself: Predict before running



Before constructing the dendrogram, use the Chapter 8 PCA and sample-distance heatmap to predict what the clustering might show. Discuss these questions with a partner before revealing the solution:

Did the HAT and SERO TL+ samples form separate, overlapping or unclear groups in the PCA?
Which samples do you predict will join at relatively low heights in the dendrogram?
Do you expect all samples with the same status to be equally similar? Why or why not?
If one sample does not appear where you expect, what information should be checked before drawing a conclusion?









TipSolution






The PCA suggested some separation between HAT and SERO TL+ samples, so samples with the same status may appear more often within the same larger branches.
Samples that appeared close in the PCA, or had small pairwise distances, may join at relatively low heights.
Samples with the same status will not necessarily be equally similar. Biological variation, sample composition, technical variation and other measured or unmeasured factors can contribute to differences among individuals.
An unexpected position does not automatically make a sample incorrect or unusable. We should compare the dendrogram with the PCA, pairwise distances, sample metadata, quality-control information and processing information before drawing a conclusion.

11.4 Reuse the Chapter 8 sample distances
In Chapter 8, we transposed the VST matrix so that samples were in rows and then we calculated the Euclidean distances between samples. We can use a similar statement to recreate the distance object required by hclust(), although we do not need to convert the result into a matrix because hclust() uses the dist object directly.

# Extract VST values for the selected HAT and SERO TL+ samples
selected_vst <- assay(selected_vsd)

# Transpose and place samples in rows
sample_by_gene <- t(selected_vst)

# Calculate the distance between every pair of samples
sample_dist <- dist(sample_by_gene)

# Inspect the first few distances
head(sample_dist)

[1] 74.00000 71.22884 75.22306 81.09497 76.75551 71.17922


A smaller distance represents more similar expression profiles.

title: 11  Pattern discovery, hierarchical clustering and heatmaps
text:
11.5 Build the sample dendrogram
Hierarchical clustering begins with each sample in its own group. It repeatedly joins samples or groups according to their distance until all samples are connected.

# Cluster samples using complete linkage
sample_hclust_all_genes <- hclust(
  sample_dist,
  method = "complete"
)

By default, hclust() uses a complete linkage method to calculate distances between groups of samples. Complete linkage compares groups using their most distant pair of samples. Other linkage methods are available and may produce different dendrograms, so the method used should be recorded when reporting the analysis.

title: 11  Pattern discovery, hierarchical clustering and heatmaps
text:
11.6 Plot the dendrogram
We can now draw the dendrogram. Unfortunately, ggplot2 doesn’t have a method for drawing dendrograms but the ggdendro package provides a ggdendrogram() helper function. It takes the specialised object created by hclust() and displays it as a figure that is compatible with ggplot2.
This is similar to our previous use of the ggrepel package. Rather than calculating all the label positions ourselves, we used the geom_label_repel() helper to position labels clearly. Here, ggdendrogram() handles the branch and sample-label positions needed to display a dendrogram.
First we have to load the package:

library(ggdendro)

We can now create and store the dendrogram using the familiar ggplot2 format:

# Create a ggplot2-compatible dendrogram
sample_dendrogram <- ggdendrogram(
  sample_hclust_all_genes,
  rotate = FALSE
)

The argument rotate = FALSE places the sample labels along the bottom of the dendrogram. Changing this to rotate = TRUE would display the dendrogram horizontally.
The dendrogram is stored as a ggplot2 object called sample_dendrogram. This means that it can be displayed and modified similarly to the other ggplot2 objects:
# Add a title to the dendrogram
sample_dendrogram <- sample_dendrogram +
  labs(
    title = "Hierarchical clustering of samples"
  )
  
# Display the dendrogram
sample_dendrogram
In the dendrogram:

Each sample name at the bottom is the end of a branch
Samples that join at relatively low heights have more similar profiles
Samples or groups that join at higher heights are less similar
The vertical merge height represents distance under the selected linkage rule
Horizontal position is not a numerical measurement
Branches can be rotated without changing which samples are grouped together

A dendrogram describes relationships but does not prove that a branch is a distinct biological subtype.

Do the main branches of the dendrogram broadly correspond to sample status? Identify any samples that do not follow the main pattern.

Why might the dendrogram, PCA plot and sample-distance heatmap show similar but not identical patterns?









TipPossible answers






The main branches may broadly correspond to sample status, although not every sample necessarily follows the dominant pattern. Samples within the same status group can still differ because of biological or technical variation.
The dendrogram makes the nested grouping of samples particularly clear. It shows which samples cluster first and how smaller groups combine into larger groups. The sample-distance heatmap shows the pairwise distances more directly, while the PCA plot shows the major directions of variation in a reduced number of dimensions.
The three visualisations summarise the expression data in different ways. The dendrogram uses the selected distance and linkage methods, the sample-distance heatmap displays pairwise distances, and PCA represents the major directions of variation. They may therefore reveal related but not identical patterns.

11.7 Joining sample clustering to a gene-expression heatmap
The sample dendrogram describes broad relationships among samples using all retained genes from the samples in the HAT-versus-SERO TL+ comparison.
To explore the underlying data further, we can use clustering to construct a gene-expression heatmap. This heatmap will show how genes prioritised by the HAT-versus-SERO TL+ differential-expression analysis behave across individual samples.
While the all-gene sample dendrogram we have made describes broad relationships among samples, this new heatmap will describe how genes vary across individual samples.
In this section:

the samples will be ordered using the hierarchical clustering calculated from all retained VST-transformed genes
the selected genes will be clustered using their standardised expression patterns across the samples

The resulting heatmap will show both the sample-clustering order and the gene-clustering order. In the next chapter, we will divide the gene dendrogram into discrete gene-expression signatures.






WarningGene selection affects the question



The heatmap genes are selected using the HAT-versus-SERO TL+ statistical comparison. Separation by status in the resulting heatmap is therefore expected and is not independent confirmation of the differential-expression result.
The heatmap is still useful for examining:

whether individual samples follow the broad pattern
whether there is variation within the status groups
whether the selected genes appear to contain one dominant response or several different patterns

It should not be presented as proof that the sample groups were discovered without using status information.

title: 11  Pattern discovery, hierarchical clustering and heatmaps
text:
11.10 Standardise expression within each gene
Genes can have very different overall expression levels but we want the heatmap colour to show whether a sample has relatively high or low expression for that gene. To do that, we can standardise the expression values within each gene by converting them to z-scores.






NoteHow z-scores are calculated





Z-scores are transformed values commonly used to compare relative expression patterns. Here, they are used for clustering and visualisation, not for differential-expression testing or for comparing absolute expression between genes.
You do not need to memorise the formula or calculate z-scores manually.
\[
z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}
\]
where:

\(x\) is the expression value for one sample;
\(\bar{x}\) is the mean expression of that gene across samples;
\(s\) is the standard deviation of that gene across samples.

For example, if a gene has a mean of 10 and a standard deviation of 2, an expression value of 12 has a z-score of:
\[
z = \frac{12 - 10}{2} = 1
\]
This means that the value is one standard deviation above that gene’s mean.



This can be difficult to follow at first but imagine that a gene has expression values of 8, 10 and 12 across three samples. The mean expression of the gene is 10 in this dataset. The value 8 is below that gene’s mean, 10 is near its mean, and 12 is above its mean.
Row standardisation converts these relationships into a value called a z-score:

Negative z-scores are below that gene’s mean in the dataset
Near zero z-scores are close to that gene’s mean in the dataset
Positive z-scores are above that gene’s mean in the dataset

A z-score does not represent absolute expression. Because each gene is standardised separately, z-scores should not be used to compare the absolute expression levels of different genes.
The supplied code standardises each gene in the overview_matrix separately and stores it in a new overview_z object. The two uses of t() temporarily place genes in columns, allowing scale() to standardise each gene across samples. You do not need to memorise the nested code.

overview_z <- t(
  scale(
    t(overview_matrix)
  )
)

We can check that the dimensions have not changed by using:

dim(overview_matrix)

[1] 150  15

dim(overview_z)

[1] 150  15








NoteWhy are there two uses of t()?





scale() operates on matrix columns but our genes are stored in rows.

The first t() temporarily places genes in columns.
scale() standardises each gene.
The second t() restores genes to rows.

title: 11  Pattern discovery, hierarchical clustering and heatmaps
text:
11.11 Cluster genes by expression pattern
When constructing the dendrogram, we clustered samples using their expression profiles across genes. We can also change the unit of analysis and cluster genes using their standardised expression patterns across samples.
In the overview_z object that contains z-score standardised data:

genes are stored in rows
samples are stored in columns

The dist() function compares rows. Applying it to overview_z therefore means it calculates the distances between genes and no additional transpose is required.

# Calculate distances between gene-expression patterns
gene_dist <- dist(
  overview_z
)

# Cluster genes using complete linkage
gene_hclust <- hclust(
  gene_dist,
  method = "complete"
)

The gene_hclust object records how genes with similar standardised expression patterns are clustered using the distance between them. We will not display the complete gene dendrogram because it contains 150 gene labels and would be difficult to read. Instead, we will just use the dendrogram to determine the order of the gene rows in the heatmap.

11.12 Retrieve the sample and gene orders
The sample and gene clustering objects each store an ordering of the labels in their hclust object.
To investigate patterns in the RNA-seq data, we can use:

the sample order to arrange the heatmap columns
the gene order to arrange the heatmap rows

The sample_order and gene_order can be extracted from the hclust objects using the following code:

sample_order <- sample_hclust_all_genes$labels[
  sample_hclust_all_genes$order
]

gene_order <- gene_hclust$labels[
  gene_hclust$order
]

title: 11  Pattern discovery, hierarchical clustering and heatmaps
text:
11.13 Prepare the heatmap plotting data
The standardised expression values are stored as z-scores in overview_z, with genes in rows and samples in columns.
To create the heatmap, we need to:

reshape the matrix into one row per heatmap tile
apply the sample order from the sample dendrogram
apply the gene order from the gene dendrogram

The following is supplied preparation code. Run the complete block, but focus on what each stage accomplishes rather than memorising the code. It is all based on concepts we have looked at in previous chapters.

# Convert the matrix into one row per gene-sample combination using as.table()
heatmap_data <- as.data.frame(
  as.table(overview_z)
)

# Change the column names to be more informative 
colnames(heatmap_data) <- c(
  "gene_id",
  "sample_id",
  "z_score"
)

# Order columns using the sample dendrogram
heatmap_data$sample_id <- factor(
  heatmap_data$sample_id,
  levels = sample_order
)

# Order rows using the gene dendrogram
heatmap_data$gene_id <- factor(
  heatmap_data$gene_id,
  levels = rev(gene_order)
)

11.14 Construct the clustered expression heatmap
We can now use geom_tile() to construct the heatmap, just as we did for the sample-distance heatmap in Chapter 8:

expression_heatmap <- ggplot(
  heatmap_data,
  aes(
    x = sample_id,
    y = gene_id,
    fill = z_score
  )
) +
  geom_tile()

expression_heatmap








In this plot:

the horizontal axis identifies the samples
the vertical axis represents the selected genes
the fill colour represents the row z-score
each tile represents one gene in one sample

The order of the heatmap axes has already been set in heatmap_data:

Columns: samples are arranged according to the sample dendrogram.
Rows: genes are arranged according to the gene dendrogram.

This places samples and genes from similar dendrogram branches near one another, making expression patterns easier to see.
We can now add the viridis colour scale and informative sample labels and make some other modifications to make the figure easier to understand:

expression_heatmap <- expression_heatmap +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "Row z-score"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Expression patterns among selected genes",
    x = "Sample",
    y = "Gene"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    ),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank()
  )

expression_heatmap














Warning



It is best to hide the individual gene labels in this figure because 150 labels would be too small to read. Their order is still retained and follows the gene dendrogram.


In this colour scale, lower z-scores indicate relatively low expression for a gene and higher z-scores indicate relatively high expression for that gene. The colours do not represent absolute expression or allow direct comparison of expression levels between different genes.






TipTry it yourself: Interpret the clustered expression heatmap



With a partner, discuss the following questions.

title: 11  Pattern discovery, hierarchical clustering and heatmaps
text:
11.16 Summary
In this chapter, you:

constructed and interpreted a sample dendrogram
compared PCA, pairwise distances and hierarchical clustering
selected and row-standardised genes for a pattern-focused heatmap
clustered genes using their expression patterns across samples
ordered the heatmap columns and rows using the sample and gene dendrograms
interpreted and saved the clustered expression heatmap

Sample clustering compared overall expression profiles among samples. Gene clustering compared the standardised expression patterns of selected genes.
The sample clustering was unsupervised because it used all retained genes without using the status labels. The gene-clustering algorithm also did not directly use status labels, but the genes supplied to it were selected using the HAT-versus-SERO TL+ comparison. The selected-gene heatmap is therefore not an independent unsupervised discovery of status separation.
The gene dendrogram shows nested relationships among genes, but it does not yet define discrete gene-expression signatures. We will investigate this further in the next session.

title: 11  Pattern discovery, hierarchical clustering and heatmaps
text:
11.17 Optional extra activities
You have now completed the required activities for this chapter. The remaining section is an optional, but valuable challenge for further practice. You can attempt it now or return to it later.
::: {.callout-tip title=“Optional Activity 1: title=”Extension: Create a labelled heatmap” collapse=“true”}
The overview heatmap is useful for identifying broad expression patterns, but it does not show the names of individual genes.
In this extension, you will repeat the same heatmap workflow using 50 genes with readable gene symbols:

select genes using adjusted p-values;
standardise expression within each gene;
cluster genes by their standardised expression patterns;
order the samples and genes using their dendrograms;
display the gene symbols on the heatmap.

This heatmap asks a more focused question:

Which individual genes show the broad expression patterns visible in the overview heatmap?


11.17.1 Select 50 genes with readable symbols
First, retain genes that have both a non-missing adjusted p-value and a readable gene symbol:

labelled_heatmap_genes <- result_data[
  !is.na(result_data$padj) &
    !is.na(result_data$symbol) &
    result_data$symbol != "",
]

Order the genes by adjusted p-value:

labelled_heatmap_genes <- labelled_heatmap_genes[
  order(labelled_heatmap_genes$padj),
]

Select the first 50 genes:

labelled_heatmap_genes <- head(
  labelled_heatmap_genes,
  50
)

More than one stable gene identifier can occasionally share the same gene symbol. Create unique display labels so that every heatmap row has a distinct label:

labelled_heatmap_genes$display_symbol <- make.unique(
  labelled_heatmap_genes$symbol
)

The adjusted p-values determine which genes are selected. Hierarchical clustering will determine the order in which they appear in the heatmap.


11.17.2 Extract and standardise the expression values
Extract the VST-transformed expression values for the selected genes:

labelled_matrix <- selected_vst[
  labelled_heatmap_genes$gene_id,
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

Check the dimensions of the resulting matrix:

dim(labelled_matrix)

[1] 50 15


The matrix should contain 50 rows, one for each selected gene.
Standardise the expression values within each gene:

labelled_z <- t(
  scale(
    t(labelled_matrix)
  )
)

The row z-scores describe expression relative to each gene’s own mean:

negative values indicate expression below that gene’s mean;
values near zero indicate expression near that gene’s mean;
positive values indicate expression above that gene’s mean.

Check that standardisation has not changed the dimensions:

dim(labelled_z)

[1] 50 15




11.17.3 Cluster the selected genes
The genes are stored in the rows of labelled_z. Therefore, dist() calculates distances between genes:

labelled_gene_dist <- dist(
  labelled_z
)

Cluster genes with similar standardised expression patterns using complete linkage:

labelled_gene_hclust <- hclust(
  labelled_gene_dist,
  method = "complete"
)

The resulting dendrogram determines the order of the gene rows in the labelled heatmap.


11.17.4 Prepare the plotting data
The following supplied code performs several preparation steps:

retrieves the gene order from the new gene dendrogram;
converts the matrix into one row per gene-sample combination;
associates each stable gene identifier with a readable symbol;
applies the sample and gene dendrogram orders.

You do not need to memorise this code. Focus on what the resulting objects control:

sample_order controls the heatmap columns;
labelled_gene_order controls the heatmap rows.


# Retrieve the gene order from the new gene dendrogram
labelled_gene_order <- labelled_gene_hclust$labels[
  labelled_gene_hclust$order
]

# Convert the matrix into one row per gene-sample combination
labelled_plot_data <- as.data.frame(
  as.table(labelled_z)
)

# Give the columns informative names
colnames(labelled_plot_data) <- c(
  "gene_id",
  "sample_id",
  "z_score"
)

# Convert the identifiers to character values before matching
labelled_plot_data$gene_id <- as.character(
  labelled_plot_data$gene_id
)

labelled_plot_data$sample_id <- as.character(
  labelled_plot_data$sample_id
)

labelled_heatmap_genes$gene_id <- as.character(
  labelled_heatmap_genes$gene_id
)

labelled_gene_order <- as.character(
  labelled_gene_order
)

# Match each stable gene identifier to its display symbol
labelled_plot_data$gene_symbol <-
  labelled_heatmap_genes$display_symbol[
    match(
      labelled_plot_data$gene_id,
      labelled_heatmap_genes$gene_id
    )
  ]

# Convert the clustered gene identifiers into display symbols
labelled_symbol_order <-
  labelled_heatmap_genes$display_symbol[
    match(
      labelled_gene_order,
      labelled_heatmap_genes$gene_id
    )
  ]

# Apply the sample dendrogram order to the heatmap columns
labelled_plot_data$sample_id <- factor(
  labelled_plot_data$sample_id,
  levels = sample_order
)

# Apply the gene dendrogram order to the heatmap rows
labelled_plot_data$gene_symbol <- factor(
  labelled_plot_data$gene_symbol,
  levels = rev(labelled_symbol_order)
)

The samples and genes are now arranged in the same way as in the overview heatmap:

the sample columns follow the sample dendrogram;
the gene rows follow the labelled-gene dendrogram.

Inspect the prepared data:

11.17.5 Construct the labelled heatmap
Construct the heatmap using the same Viridis scale and plotting approach as the overview heatmap:

labelled_heatmap <- ggplot(
  labelled_plot_data,
  aes(
    x = sample_id,
    y = gene_symbol,
    fill = z_score
  )
) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "Row z-score"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Expression patterns among selected genes",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Samples and genes are ordered",
      "using hierarchical clustering"
    ),

Before looking at the suggested solution, think about the following questions:

Which broad patterns are easier to see in the 150-gene overview heatmap?
Which individual genes are easier to investigate in the labelled heatmap?
Does reducing the number of genes alter the apparent sample pattern?
What is gained and lost by displaying individual gene symbols?
Why might the gene order differ between the two heatmaps?
Do the two heatmaps provide independent evidence of differences between HAT and SERO TL+ samples? Why or why not?







NotePossible answers






The 150-gene overview heatmap includes more information and may make large groups of genes with similar expression patterns easier to identify.
The labelled heatmap makes it possible to identify individual genes associated with particular expression patterns.
The broad sample pattern may remain similar, but some details may change because the labelled heatmap uses a smaller set of genes.
Displaying gene symbols makes individual genes easier to identify, but it limits how many genes can be shown clearly and can make broad patterns harder to see.
The heatmaps contain different sets of genes. Hierarchical clustering is calculated separately for each set, so the gene distances, dendrogram branches and resulting row orders may differ.
No. Both heatmaps use genes selected from the same HAT-versus-SERO TL+ differential-expression comparison. They visualise patterns among prioritised genes but do not provide independent evidence of differences between the status groups.

The sample dendrogram and expression heatmap show related information:

the dendrogram shows the relationships among samples;
the heatmap shows the standardised expression patterns;
the order of the heatmap columns follows the leaves of the sample dendrogram.

In this extension, you will use patchwork to place the sample dendrogram directly above the corresponding heatmap columns.

11.17.8 Load the required packages
We will use:

ggdendro to convert the hierarchical-clustering result into data that can be plotted with ggplot2;
patchwork to arrange the dendrogram and heatmap vertically.

Install these packages once if they are not already installed:
install.packages("ggdendro")
install.packages("patchwork")
Load the packages:

library(ggdendro)
library(patchwork)



11.17.9 Prepare the dendrogram data
The sample clustering is stored in:
sample_hclust_all_genes
Convert this clustering result into data that can be plotted with ggplot2:

sample_dendrogram_data <- dendro_data(
  sample_hclust_all_genes,
  type = "rectangle"
)

The horizontal position of each dendrogram leaf corresponds to the position of a sample in sample_order.


11.17.10 Construct the sample dendrogram
Use the segment information to draw the dendrogram:

sample_dendrogram_aligned <- ggplot(
  segment(sample_dendrogram_data)
) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      xend = xend,
      yend = yend
    ),
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(
      0.5,
      length(sample_order) + 0.5
    ),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    expand = expansion(
      mult = c(0, 0.05)
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    y = "Distance"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.title.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    plot.margin = margin(
      t = 5,
      r = 5,
      b = 0,
      l = 5
    )
  )

sample_dendrogram_aligned








The sample labels are omitted from the dendrogram because they will be shown on the heatmap below.


11.17.11 Construct a heatmap for the combined figure
Construct the heatmap using the same data, sample order and Viridis scale as the main heatmap:

heatmap_aligned <- ggplot(
  heatmap_data,
  aes(
    x = sample_id,
    y = gene_id,
    fill = z_score
  )
) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_x_discrete(
    expand = expansion(
      add = 0.5
    )
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "Row z-score"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Sample",
    y = "Selected genes"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    ),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    plot.margin = margin(
      t = 0,
      r = 5,
      b = 5,
      l = 5
    )
