heatmap_aligned








The dendrogram and heatmap use the same sample order:

the dendrogram leaves follow sample_order;
the heatmap columns use sample_order as their factor-level order.

The x-axis limits also provide half a position of space on either side. This helps align the centres of the dendrogram leaves with the centres of the heatmap columns.


11.17.12 Combine the dendrogram and heatmap
Use the / operator from patchwork to place the dendrogram above the heatmap:

heatmap_with_dendrogram <- (
  sample_dendrogram_aligned /
    heatmap_aligned
) +
  plot_layout(
    heights = c(1, 4)
  ) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Clustered expression patterns across samples"
  )

heatmap_with_dendrogram







Figure 11.4





The values supplied to heights determine how the available vertical space is divided:
heights = c(1, 4)
This gives one part of the available height to the dendrogram and four parts to the heatmap.


11.17.13 Check the alignment
Examine the combined figure and consider:

Does each dendrogram leaf align with the centre of a heatmap column?
Can you follow major dendrogram branches into corresponding groups of heatmap columns?
Does adding the dendrogram make the sample relationships easier to interpret?
Is the dendrogram large enough to read without taking too much space from the heatmap?
What information does the dendrogram add that is not shown by the heatmap alone?







NotePossible answers






Each dendrogram leaf should align with the centre of one heatmap column because both panels use the same sample order.
Major dendrogram branches should correspond to adjacent groups of heatmap columns. The heatmap can then be used to examine the expression patterns associated with those branches.
The dendrogram makes the hierarchical relationships among the samples explicit. The heatmap alone displays the samples in clustered order but does not show where branches join.
The relative panel heights can be changed if either panel is difficult to read. For example, heights = c(1.5, 4) would provide more space for the dendrogram.
The dendrogram shows the nested grouping of samples and the relative heights at which branches join. The heatmap shows the standardised expression patterns underlying the visual comparison.

  filename = "figures/heatmap_with_sample_dendrogram.png",
  plot = heatmap_with_dendrogram

title: 12  Gene-expression signatures
text:
What you’ll learn In Chapter 11, you used hierarchical clustering to arrange samples and genes according to their expression patterns. You then used the clustering results to construct a gene-expression heatmap.
The heatmap suggested that the selected genes do not all follow the same expression pattern. Some genes may be relatively higher in HAT samples, others may be relatively higher in SERO TL+ samples, and some may show more variable patterns among individual samples.
In this chapter, we will convert these visual patterns into reproducible groups of genes called gene-expression signatures.
We will first divide the gene dendrogram into a selected number of groups. We will then introduce k-means clustering as an alternative method for assigning genes to groups and compare the results produced by the two approaches.
Finally, we will inspect the expression pattern represented by each signature and save separate gene lists for functional enrichment analysis in Chapter 11.
::: {.callout-important title=“Research question”} Can we identify reproducible groups of genes that share similar expression patterns across the HAT and SERO TL+ samples? :::






NoteLearning outcomes



By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:
explain why a heatmap may contain several distinct gene-expression patterns; use cutree() to divide a hierarchical gene tree into a selected number of groups; explain the difference between hierarchical clustering and k-means clustering; explain why k-means requires the number of clusters to be selected in advance; run k-means reproducibly using set.seed() and multiple starting positions; compare gene assignments produced by hierarchical clustering and k-means; inspect the expression pattern associated with each gene cluster; explain why cluster numbers are arbitrary labels rather than biological rankings; describe gene clusters using their observed expression patterns; evaluate how the selected number of clusters affects the result; create and export a gene-signature membership table; prepare separate gene lists for functional enrichment analysis in Chapter 11. ISCB competency framework v3 alignment: B3, D3, E3, F3 and H3, mainly at application level. The session emphasises applying clustering methods, comparing analytical choices, inspecting high-dimensional expression patterns, producing reproducible gene lists and making cautious biological interpretations.

In Chapter 5, you connected the Ensembl identifiers in the differential-expression results to the supplied human annotation table using match(). That table also contains Entrez identifiers. 13.2 Session route map
This session is designed for approximately 150 minutes:

Reconnect with the biological question and predict (15 min)
Retrieve and verify the Chapter 5 annotated result (20 min)
Reuse and audit the identifier annotation (15 min)
Define the ORA universe and directional gene sets (25 min)
Run and inspect HAT enrichment (30 min)
Repeat for SERO TL+ and compare themes (25 min)

Chapter 5 annotation → mapped tested genes → directional gene list + tested-gene universe → ORA → term-level and gene-level inspection → cautious biological hypothesis

title: 13  Functional Enrichment Analysis
text:
13.3 1. Reconnect with earlier chapters
Chapter 4 fitted the DESeq2 model and defined the contrast as HAT versus SERO TL+. Chapter 5 then explored and annotated that result. For this contrast:

a positive log2FoldChange means higher estimated expression in HAT;
a negative log2FoldChange means higher estimated expression in SERO TL+;
padj describes statistical evidence after correcting for testing many genes.

Chapters 9 and 10 showed that many prioritised genes form coordinated expression patterns. Functional enrichment now provides a systematic way to ask whether the selected genes share more biological-process annotations than expected from the genes that could have been selected.






TipPRIMM activity 1: Predict



Before running new code, discuss:

If symptomatic HAT is associated with altered host immune activity, which broad biological themes might be enriched among genes higher in HAT?
Would every gene assigned to an enriched term need to have the same fold change?
Would enrichment of an immune-related term prove that immune activity caused the clinical difference?
Why might genes higher in SERO TL+ reveal different themes rather than simply the opposite list?

Record one prediction:
# We predict that genes higher in HAT may be enriched for __________
# because earlier chapters showed __________.
# This would suggest __________, but would not demonstrate __________.








NoteBiological context



HAT is caused by Trypanosoma parasites. In this dataset, HAT samples are from symptomatic participants, whereas SERO TL+ samples are serology-positive without the overt HAT phenotype. Expression differences may reflect immune responses, infection stage, parasite burden, circulating cell composition, participant heterogeneity or technical factors. The analysis therefore identifies associations with the sampled clinical groups rather than a controlled transition between states.

ImportantPartner comparison task



For each direction, select up to three informative terms and record:

Observation: term, gene ratio, count and adjusted p-value;
Gene-level evidence: contributing genes and overlap among terms;
Biological interpretation: a plausible connection to symptomatic HAT or SERO TL+;
Alternative explanation: cell composition, age, infection stage, parasite burden, sample processing or another unmeasured variable;
Next step: a measurement or analysis that could distinguish between explanations.

Use associated with, consistent with, suggests or motivates the hypothesis that. Avoid causes, proves and the pathway is activated.

13.12 10. Connect enrichment to Chapters 9 and 10
Chapters 9 and 10 grouped genes using similarity in their expression patterns. ORA groups genes because they share curated functional annotations. These provide different forms of evidence.






TipPearson reasoning task



Discuss:

Can two genes share a GO term without having strongly correlated expression?
Can two strongly correlated genes lack a shared GO annotation?
What evidence comes from co-expression, and what evidence comes from annotation?
Why is agreement between an expression signature and an enriched theme interesting but not independent proof of a mechanism?
Which Chapter 10 signatures contain genes contributing to the selected enriched terms?

NoteLearning outcomes



By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

distinguish an omnibus likelihood-ratio test from a directional pairwise contrast

library(DESeq2); library(ggplot2); library(pheatmap)

count_data <- as.matrix(read.csv("m_sample_counts.csv", header = TRUE, row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE))
sample_info <- read.csv("m_sample_info.csv", header = TRUE, row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
sample_info <- sample_info[colnames(count_data), , drop = FALSE]
sample_info$status <- factor(sample_info$status)

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = count_data, colData = sample_info, design = ~ status)
dds <- dds[rowSums(counts(dds)) >= 10, ]

gene_annotation <- data.frame(gene_id = rownames(dds), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
annotation_file <- read.csv("human_annotations_from_orgHs.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
gene_annotation$symbol <- annotation_file$SYMBOL_SAFE[match(gene_annotation$gene_id, annotation_file$ENSEMBL)]
missing_symbol <- is.na(gene_annotation$symbol) | gene_annotation$symbol == ""
gene_annotation$symbol[missing_symbol] <- gene_annotation$gene_id[missing_symbol]

dds <- DESeq(dds)
res_hat_vs_sero <- results(dds, contrast = c("status", "hat", "sero"), alpha = 0.05)

vsd <- vst(dds, blind = FALSE)
vst_values <- assay(vsd)

GROUP_COLOURS <- c(

14.2 The omnibus test: all three groups at once
Every contrast so far has compared exactly two groups. To ask “does this gene differ across any of the three groups?” we need a different kind of test: a Likelihood Ratio Test (LRT), which compares our full model against a reduced model with no group effect at all.

dds_lrt <- DESeq(dds, test = "LRT", reduced = ~ 1)
res_all_groups <- results(dds_lrt, alpha = 0.05)







ImportantCheck your understanding



A significant LRT result tells you that status improves the model fit for that gene. Does it tell you which pair of groups differs, or in which direction? What further result would you need to answer those two questions?






TipSolution





No — the LRT only tests whether some difference exists among the three groups; it does not identify which pair differs, or which direction the difference runs. To answer those questions you need a directional pairwise contrast, exactly like the HAT-vs-SERO contrast from Chapter 4.






lrt_data <- as.data.frame(res_all_groups)
res_all_groups_table <- data.frame(
  gene_id = rownames(lrt_data),
  symbol = gene_annotation$symbol[match(rownames(lrt_data), gene_annotation$gene_id)],
  lrt_data, row.names = NULL, check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
res_all_groups_table <- res_all_groups_table[order(res_all_groups_table$padj), ]

write.csv(res_all_groups_table, file.path("results", "tables", "T12_omnibus_all_groups.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

14.5 Comparing all three pairwise contrasts
We already have HAT vs SERO. Let’s extract the other two contrasts.

res_sero_vs_ctrl <- results(dds, contrast = c("status", "sero", "ctrl"), alpha = 0.05)
res_hat_vs_ctrl <- results(dds, contrast = c("status", "hat", "ctrl"), alpha = 0.05)

A small helper function avoids repeating the same annotation-and-sort code three times:

format_de_table <- function(result) {
  result_data <- as.data.frame(result)
  result_table <- data.frame(
    gene_id = rownames(result_data),
    symbol = gene_annotation$symbol[match(rownames(result_data), gene_annotation$gene_id)],
    result_data, row.names = NULL, check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  result_table[order(result_table$padj, na.last = TRUE), ]
}

write.csv(format_de_table(res_sero_vs_ctrl), file.path("results", "tables", "T12_DE_sero_vs_ctrl.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(format_de_table(res_hat_vs_ctrl), file.path("results", "tables", "T12_DE_hat_vs_ctrl.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

Next, a helper to extract just the significant gene IDs from any result, using a consistent rule:

get_significant_genes <- function(result, padj_cutoff = 0.05, lfc_cutoff = 1) {
  result_data <- as.data.frame(result)
  keep <- !is.na(result_data$padj) &
    result_data$padj < padj_cutoff &
    abs(result_data$log2FoldChange) > lfc_cutoff
  rownames(result_data)[keep]
}

sig_hat_vs_sero <- get_significant_genes(res_hat_vs_sero)
sig_sero_vs_ctrl <- get_significant_genes(res_sero_vs_ctrl)
sig_hat_vs_ctrl <- get_significant_genes(res_hat_vs_ctrl)

14.6 A bar chart of overlapping gene sets
A three-set Venn/Euler diagram can distort area to approximate overlap size, which makes it easy to misread. A bar chart shows the exact count for each overlap category instead.

sig_any <- union(union(sig_hat_vs_sero, sig_sero_vs_ctrl), sig_hat_vs_ctrl)
sig_all_three <- Reduce(intersect, list(sig_hat_vs_sero, sig_sero_vs_ctrl, sig_hat_vs_ctrl))

sig_hat_vs_sero_only <- setdiff(sig_hat_vs_sero, union(sig_sero_vs_ctrl, sig_hat_vs_ctrl))
sig_sero_vs_ctrl_only <- setdiff(sig_sero_vs_ctrl, union(sig_hat_vs_sero, sig_hat_vs_ctrl))
sig_hat_vs_ctrl_only <- setdiff(sig_hat_vs_ctrl, union(sig_hat_vs_sero, sig_sero_vs_ctrl))

overlap_lists <- list(
  sig_any = sig_any,
  sig_all_three = sig_all_three,
  sig_hat_vs_sero_only = sig_hat_vs_sero_only,
  sig_sero_vs_ctrl_only = sig_sero_vs_ctrl_only,
  sig_hat_vs_ctrl_only = sig_hat_vs_ctrl_only
)

overlap_summary <- data.frame(
  category = names(overlap_lists),
  n_genes = vapply(overlap_lists, length, integer(1))
)

14.7 Stretch goals and where to go next
Everything up to this point forms the core analysis. If you’d like to go further:

GSEA (Gene Set Enrichment Analysis) uses the whole ranked gene list instead of a significance cutoff, and can reveal subtler, coordinated shifts in expression.
STRING network analysis visualises known protein–protein interactions among your candidate genes.
A sensitivity analysis, re-running your filtering threshold, significance cutoff, or clustering value \(k\) and reporting how conclusions change (or don’t).
An independently chosen contrast or dataset, applying this same workflow end-to-end.
